extraction_notes.note: Proposition 3.1 is attributed to Karpov-Nogin and Auel-Bernardara for smooth X; the du Val extension is left to the reader, so it is kept origin paper with rigor semi_formal rather than external.
Theorem B.1 is stated as communicated by J. Tevelev, so it is marked external although the paper supplies the proof.
Remark or claim: the paragraph argues and concludes (the decomposition extends to D^-) in one go and also introduces the components A~_i^-; kept as a remark.

Corollary 5.5 is introduced by an unpunctuated lead-in sentence ('Considering base changes ... we obtain') that runs into the environment; no proof node was made, uses edges from Theorem 4.5 and Lemma 5.4 instead.
The parser marks only the third item of the first itemize in the proof of Lemma 6.1 as an author label, so a step starts there while the first two items stay inside the preceding step.
The introduction's informal restatements of the main results, the tables/figures of curve configurations and toric polygons, and local notation such as S_0 := S minus S_1 were not made nodes.
Several results state their content as type-by-type tables inside equation* arrays; kept verbatim inside the result statements.

nodes.statement: Throughout the paper we work over a field ${\mathsf{k}}$, whose characteristic is assumed to be distinct from~2 and~3.
nodes.name: Characteristic of the base field

nodes.statement: In sections~\ref{section:preliminaries}, \ref{section:dp6-single} and~\ref{section:moduli-spaces} we assume that ${\mathsf{k}}$ is algebraically closed, while in sections~\ref{section:families} and~\ref{section:special-families} we leave this assumption.
nodes.name: Algebraically closed base field in Sections 2-4

nodes.statement: For a scheme $X$ we denote by ${\mathbf{D}}(X)$ the bounded derived category of coherent sheaves on $X$, and unless something else is specified explicitly, this is what we mean by a derived category.
nodes.name: Bounded derived category D(X)

nodes.statement: For a Brauer class $\beta$ on a scheme $X$ we denote by ${\mathbf{D}}(X,\beta)$ the twisted bounded derived category of coherent sheaves.
nodes.name: Twisted derived category D(X,beta)

nodes.statement: A {\sf sextic du Val del Pezzo surface} is a normal integral projective surface $X$ over a field ${\mathsf{k}}$ with at worst du Val singularities and ample anticanonical class such that $K_X^2 = 6$.
nodes.name: Sextic du Val del Pezzo surface
nodes.definiendum: sextic du Val del Pezzo surface
nodes.genus: normal integral projective surface $X$ over a field ${\mathsf{k}}$
differentia: with at worst du Val singularities
nodes.label: definition:dp6

nodes.statement: Let $\pi \colon {\widetilde{X}} \to X$ be the minimal (in particular crepant) resolution of singularities of $X$.
nodes.name: Minimal resolution pi: X~ -> X

nodes.statement: It is well-known (see, e.g.~\cite[Section~8.4.2]{dolgachev2012cag}) that the surface ${\widetilde{X}}$ is rational and can be obtained from ${\mathbb{P}}^2$ by a sequence of three blowups of a point, i.e., we have a diagram \begin{equation*} X \xleftarrow{\ \pi\ } {\widetilde{X}} = X_3 \to X_2 \to X_1 \to X_0 = {\mathbb{P}}^2, \end{equation*} where each map $X_i \to X_{i-1}$ is the blowup of a point $P_i \in X_{i-1}$.
nodes.name: Minimal resolution of a sextic del Pezzo surface as a triple blowup of P^2
nodes.statement_short: The minimal resolution X~ is rational, obtained from P^2 by three successive point blowups.
conclusions: the surface ${\widetilde{X}}$ is rational and can be obtained from ${\mathbb{P}}^2$ by a sequence of three blowups of a point

nodes.statement: We denote by $h$ the hyperplane class on ${\mathbb{P}}^2$ and its pullback to ${\widetilde{X}}$.
nodes.name: Hyperplane class h

nodes.statement: We denote by $E_i \subset {\widetilde{X}}$ the pullback (i.e., the total preimage) to ${\widetilde{X}}$ of the exceptional divisor of $X_i \to X_{i-1}$ and by $e_i$ its class in $\mathrm{Pic}({\widetilde{X}})$.
nodes.name: Exceptional divisors E_i and classes e_i

nodes.statement: We have $\mathrm{Pic}({\widetilde{X}}) \cong {\mathbb{Z}}\langle h, e_1,e_2,e_3 \rangle$, with $h^2 = 1$, $e_i^2 = -1$, $he_i = e_ie_j = 0$ for all $i \ne j$. Moreover, \begin{equation} K_{\widetilde{X}} = -3h + e_1 + e_2 + e_3 = \pi^*K_X. \end{equation}
nodes.name: Picard group of the weak del Pezzo resolution
nodes.statement_short: Pic of the resolution is Z<h,e1,e2,e3> with standard intersection form and K = -3h+e1+e2+e3 = pi^*K_X.
conclusions: $\mathrm{Pic}({\widetilde{X}}) \cong {\mathbb{Z}}\langle h, e_1,e_2,e_3 \rangle$, with $h^2 = 1$, $e_i^2 = -1$, $he_i = e_ie_j = 0$ for all $i \ne j$
nodes.label: lemma:pic-tx

nodes.statement: K_{\widetilde{X}} = -3h + e_1 + e_2 + e_3 = \pi^*K_X.
nodes.name: Equation (1) ktx
nodes.label: eq:ktx

nodes.statement: By~\cite[Section~8.4.2]{dolgachev2012cag} there are six possibilities for configurations of the blowup centers and $(-2)$-curves on ${\widetilde{X}}$ (see Table~\ref{table:dp6} below for a picture). \begin{description} \item[Type 0] Neither of $P_i$ lies on the exceptional divisor in $X_{i-1}$ and their images in ${\mathbb{P}}^2$ do not lie on a common line. Then ${\widetilde{X}}$ contains no $(-2)$-curves and $X = {\widetilde{X}}$ is smooth. \item[Type 1] Neither of $P_i$ lies on the exceptional divisor in $X_{i-1}$ but their images in ${\mathbb{P}}^2$ lie on a common line. Then ${\widetilde{X}}$ contains a unique $(-2)$-curve (the strict transform $\Delta_{123}$ of that line) and~$X$ has one~$A_1$ singularity. \item[Type 2] The point $P_2$ lies on the exceptional divisor of $X_1 \to X_0$, the point $P_3$ is away from the exceptional divisors, and the line through $P_1$ in the direction of $P_2$ on ${\mathbb{P}}^2$ does not pass through the image of $P_3$. Then ${\widetilde{X}}$ contains a unique $(-2)$-curve (the strict transform $\Delta_{12}$ of the exceptional divisor of $X_1 \to X_0$) and $X$ has one $A_1$ singularity. \item[Type 3] The point $P_2$ lies on the exceptional divisor of $X_1 \to X_0$, the point $P_3$ is away from the exceptional divisors, but the line through $P_1$ in the direction of $P_2$ on ${\mathbb{P}}^2$ passes through the image of $P_3$. Then ${\widetilde{X}}$ contains two disjoint $(-2)$-curves (the strict transforms $\Delta_{123}$ and $\Delta_{12}$ of the line on~${\mathbb{P}}^2$ and of the exceptional divisor of $X_1 \to X_0$, respectively) and $X$ has two $A_1$ singularities. \item[Type 4] The point $P_2$ lies on the exceptional divisor of $X_1 \to X_0$, the point $P_3$ lies on the exceptional divisor of $X_2 \to X_1$, and the strict transform $L_{12}$ of the line through $P_1$ in the direction of $P_2$ does not contain $P_3$. Then ${\widetilde{X}}$ contains a 2-chain of $(-2)$-curves (the strict transforms $\Delta_{12}$ and $\Delta_{23}$ of the exceptional divisors of $X_1 \to X_0$ and $X_2 \to X_1$, respectively) and $X$ has one $A_2$ singularity. \item[Type 5] The point $P_2$ lies on the exceptional divisor of $X_1 \to X_0$, the point $P_3$ lies on the exceptional divisor of $X_2 \to X_1$, and the strict transform of the line through $P_1$ in the direction of $P_2$ contains $P_3$. Then ${\widetilde{X}}$ contains a 2-chain of $(-2)$-curves and one more $(-2)$-curve disjoint from the chain (the strict transforms $\Delta_{123}$, $\Delta_{12}$ and $\Delta_{23}$ of the line and the exceptional divisors of~$X_1 \to X_0$ and $X_2 \to X_1$ respectively) and $X$ has one $A_2$ singularity and one $A_1$ singularity. \end{description}
nodes.name: Classification of sextic du Val del Pezzo surfaces (types 0-5)
nodes.statement_short: Six configuration types 0-5 of blowup centers and (-2)-curves, with singularities none, A1, A1, 2A1, A2, A2+A1.
conclusions: there are six possibilities for configurations of the blowup centers and $(-2)$-curves on ${\widetilde{X}}$

nodes.statement: We denote by~${\boldsymbol\Delta} = {\boldsymbol\Delta}(X)$ the set of all $(-2)$-curves on ${\widetilde{X}}$.
nodes.name: Set of (-2)-curves Delta(X)

nodes.statement: Note that the $(-2)$ curves (when they exist) on ${\widetilde{X}}$ are contained in the following linear systems: \begin{equation*} \Delta_{12} = E_1 - E_2 \in |e_1 - e_2|, \qquad \Delta_{23} = E_2 - E_3 \in |e_2 - e_3|, \qquad\text{and}\qquad \Delta_{123} \in |h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3|.
nodes.name: Linear systems of the (-2)-curves

nodes.statement: We denote by $L_{ij}$ the strict transform of the line connecting (the images on ${\mathbb{P}}^2$ of) the points $P_i$ and $P_j$.
nodes.name: Lines L_ij

nodes.statement: In each of these types there is a unique (up to isomorphism) sextic del Pezzo surface.
nodes.name: Uniqueness of the surface of each type
conclusions: In each of these types there is a unique (up to isomorphism) sextic del Pezzo surface

nodes.statement: Moreover, the surfaces of types $0$, $2$, $3$, and $5$ are toric (in particular, the surface of type~5 is the weighted projective plane~${\mathbb{P}}(1,2,3)$, see~\cite[Example~5.8]{kawamata2015multi} for an alternative description of its derived category). The surfaces of type~1 and~4 are not toric.
nodes.name: Toric sextic del Pezzo surfaces
conclusions: the surfaces of types $0$, $2$, $3$, and $5$ are toric

nodes.statement: Denote by ${\boldsymbol\Delta}$ the set of irreducible components of the exceptional divisor of $\pi$; each of these is a smooth rational curve on ${\widetilde{X}}$.
nodes.name: Exceptional components Delta of a resolution

nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a normal surface with rational singularities and let $\pi \colon {\widetilde{X}} \to X$ be its resolution. The functor $\pi^* \colon {\mathbf{D}}^-(X) \to {\mathbf{D}}^-({\widetilde{X}})$ is fully faithful. The functor $\pi_* \colon {\mathbf{D}}^-({\widetilde{X}}) \to {\mathbf{D}}^-(X)$ is its right adjoint, it preserves boundedness, and there is an isomorphism of functors \begin{equation} \pi_* \circ \pi^* \cong \mathrm{id}. \end{equation} Moreover, \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Im} \pi^* = {}^\perp\langle {\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1) \rangle_{\Delta \in {\boldsymbol\Delta}} \qquad\text{and}\qquad \mathrm{Ker} \pi_* = \langle {\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1) \rangle^\oplus_{\Delta \in {\boldsymbol\Delta}}, \end{equation*} where $\langle - \rangle^\oplus$ denotes the minimal triangulated subcategory closed under infinite direct sums defined in ${\mathbf{D}}^-$.
nodes.name: Pullback and pushforward for a rational resolution
nodes.statement_short: For a rational resolution, pi^* is fully faithful on D^-, pi_* pi^* = id, and Ker pi_* is generated by the O_Delta(-1).
assumptions: $X$ be a normal surface with rational singularities
$\pi \colon {\widetilde{X}} \to X$ be its resolution
conclusions: The functor $\pi^* \colon {\mathbf{D}}^-(X) \to {\mathbf{D}}^-({\widetilde{X}})$ is fully faithful
nodes.label: lemma:pi-properties

nodes.statement: \pi_* \circ \pi^* \cong \mathrm{id}.
nodes.name: Equation (2) pis-pis-id
nodes.label: eq:pis-pis-id

nodes.statement: The pullback-pushforward adjunction is standard. By projection formula we have \begin{equation*} \pi_*(\pi^*{\mathscr{F}}) \cong {\mathscr{F}} \otimes \pi_*{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}, \end{equation*} and since $X$ has rational singularities, the canonical morphism ${\mathscr{O}}_X \to \pi_*{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}$ is an isomorphism, hence~\eqref{eq:pis-pis-id} holds. By adjunction it follows that $\pi^*$ is fully faithful. Finally, by~\cite[Lemma~2.1]{bodzenta2015flops} (see also~\cite[Lemma~3.1]{bridgeland} and Lemma~\ref{lemma:spectral} below) and~\cite[Proposition~9.14 and Theorem~9.15]{bodzenta2015flops} the category $\mathrm{Ker}\pi_*$ is generated by sheaves ${\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1)$. The description of $\mathrm{Im}\pi^*$ follows by adjunction.
nodes.statement_short: Adjunction plus projection formula; kernel of pi_* from Bodzenta-Bondal.
nodes.name: Proof of Pullback and pushforward for a rational resolution
Recall the adjunction
nodes.statement: The pullback-pushforward adjunction is standard.
nodes.statement_short: Recall the adjunction

nodes.name: Projection formula and rationality give pi_* pi^* = id, so pi^* is fully faithful
nodes.statement: By projection formula we have \begin{equation*} \pi_*(\pi^*{\mathscr{F}}) \cong {\mathscr{F}} \otimes \pi_*{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}, \end{equation*} and since $X$ has rational singularities, the canonical morphism ${\mathscr{O}}_X \to \pi_*{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}$ is an isomorphism, hence~\eqref{eq:pis-pis-id} holds. By adjunction it follows that $\pi^*$ is fully faithful.
nodes.statement_short: Projection formula and rationality give pi_* pi^* = id, so pi^* is fully faithful

nodes.name: Kernel of pi_* generated by O_Delta(-1); image of pi^* by adjunction
nodes.statement: Finally, by~\cite[Lemma~2.1]{bodzenta2015flops} (see also~\cite[Lemma~3.1]{bridgeland} and Lemma~\ref{lemma:spectral} below) and~\cite[Proposition~9.14 and Theorem~9.15]{bodzenta2015flops} the category $\mathrm{Ker}\pi_*$ is generated by sheaves ${\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1)$. The description of $\mathrm{Im}\pi^*$ follows by adjunction.
nodes.statement_short: Kernel of pi_* generated by O_Delta(-1); image of pi^* by adjunction

nodes.statement: Let $\pi \colon {\widetilde{X}} \to X$ be a proper morphism with fibers of dimension at most~$1$. Let ${\mathscr{F}}$ be a possibly unbounded complex of quasicoherent sheaves on ${\widetilde{X}}$ and let ${\mathscr{H}}^i({\mathscr{F}})$ be its cohomology sheaf in degree $i$. The spectral sequence $R^i\pi_*({\mathscr{H}}^j({\mathscr{F}})) \Rightarrow {\mathscr{H}}^{i+j}(\pi_*({\mathscr{F}}))$ degenerates at the second page, and gives for each $i$ an exact sequence \begin{equation*} 0 \to R^1\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i-1}({\mathscr{F}}) \to {\mathscr{H}}^i(\pi_*({\mathscr{F}})) \to R^0\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^i({\mathscr{F}}) \to 0. \end{equation*} In particular, if ${\mathscr{H}}^i(\pi_*({\mathscr{F}})) = 0$ for $i \le p$ for some integer $p$, then $\pi_*({\mathscr{H}}^i({\mathscr{F}})) = 0$ for $i \le p - 1$ and \begin{equation*} \pi_*{\mathscr{F}} \cong \pi_*(\tau^{\ge p}{\mathscr{F}}), \end{equation*} where $\tau$ stands for the truncation functor with respect to the canonical filtration.
nodes.name: Bridgeland's spectral sequence lemma
nodes.statement_short: For a proper map with fibers of dimension at most 1 the pushforward spectral sequence degenerates at E2, giving short exact sequences of cohomology sheaves.
assumptions: $\pi \colon {\widetilde{X}} \to X$ be a proper morphism with fibers of dimension at most~$1$
conclusions: The spectral sequence $R^i\pi_*({\mathscr{H}}^j({\mathscr{F}})) \Rightarrow {\mathscr{H}}^{i+j}(\pi_*({\mathscr{F}}))$ degenerates at the second page
nodes.label: lemma:spectral

nodes.statement: The fibers of $\pi$ are at most 1-dimensional, hence $R^{\ge 2}\pi_* = 0$, and the second page of the spectral sequence looks like \begin{equation*} \xymatrix@R=1ex{ \dots & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \dots \\ \dots & R^1\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i-2}({\mathscr{F}}) & R^1\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i-1}({\mathscr{F}}) & R^1\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i}({\mathscr{F}}) & R^1\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i+1}({\mathscr{F}}) & \dots \\ \dots & R^0\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i-2}({\mathscr{F}}) & R^0\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i-1}({\mathscr{F}}) \ar[uul]_{d_2} & R^0\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i}({\mathscr{F}}) \ar[uul]_{d_2} & R^0\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i+1}({\mathscr{F}}) \ar[uul]_{d_2} & \dots } \end{equation*} It follows that the spectral sequence degenerates at the second page, and gives the required exact sequences. The vanishing of $\pi_*({\mathscr{H}}^i({\mathscr{F}}))$ for all $i \le p-1$ follows immediately from the exact sequences, and in its turn implies $\pi_*(\tau^{\le p-1}{\mathscr{F}}) = 0$. Applying the pushforward to the canonical truncation triangle~$\tau^{\le p-1}{\mathscr{F}} \to {\mathscr{F}} \to \tau^{\ge p}{\mathscr{F}}$ we obtain the required isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Fibers of dimension at most one kill R^{>=2}, so the spectral sequence degenerates at E2.
nodes.name: Proof of Bridgeland's spectral sequence lemma
Only two nonzero rows in the E2 page
nodes.statement: The fibers of $\pi$ are at most 1-dimensional, hence $R^{\ge 2}\pi_* = 0$, and the second page of the spectral sequence looks like \begin{equation*} \xymatrix@R=1ex{ \dots & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \dots \\ \dots & R^1\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i-2}({\mathscr{F}}) & R^1\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i-1}({\mathscr{F}}) & R^1\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i}({\mathscr{F}}) & R^1\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i+1}({\mathscr{F}}) & \dots \\ \dots & R^0\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i-2}({\mathscr{F}}) & R^0\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i-1}({\mathscr{F}}) \ar[uul]_{d_2} & R^0\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i}({\mathscr{F}}) \ar[uul]_{d_2} & R^0\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i+1}({\mathscr{F}}) \ar[uul]_{d_2} & \dots } \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Only two nonzero rows in the E2 page

nodes.name: Degeneration gives the exact sequences and the vanishing
nodes.statement: It follows that the spectral sequence degenerates at the second page, and gives the required exact sequences. The vanishing of $\pi_*({\mathscr{H}}^i({\mathscr{F}}))$ for all $i \le p-1$ follows immediately from the exact sequences, and in its turn implies $\pi_*(\tau^{\le p-1}{\mathscr{F}}) = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Degeneration gives the exact sequences and the vanishing

nodes.name: Push forward the truncation triangle
nodes.statement: Applying the pushforward to the canonical truncation triangle~$\tau^{\le p-1}{\mathscr{F}} \to {\mathscr{F}} \to \tau^{\ge p}{\mathscr{F}}$ we obtain the required isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Push forward the truncation triangle

nodes.statement: The functor $\pi_* \colon {\mathbf{D}}({\widetilde{X}}) \to {\mathbf{D}}(X)$ is essentially surjective.
nodes.name: Essential surjectivity of pi_*
conclusions: The functor $\pi_* \colon {\mathbf{D}}({\widetilde{X}}) \to {\mathbf{D}}(X)$ is essentially surjective
nodes.label: corollary:pis-epi

nodes.statement: Let ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathbf{D}}(X)$ and assume that $p$ is such that $\tau^{\le p}({\mathscr{F}}) = 0$. Then ${\mathscr{F}} \cong \pi_*(\pi^*{\mathscr{F}}) \cong \pi_*(\tau^{\ge p}\pi^*{\mathscr{F}})$, and clearly $\tau^{\ge p}\pi^*{\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathbf{D}}({\widetilde{X}})$.
nodes.statement_short: Pull back, truncate, and push forward.
nodes.name: Proof of Essential surjectivity of pi_*

nodes.statement: Let $f \colon X \to Y$ be a proper morphism. The {\sf Grothendieck duality} is a bifunctorial isomorphism \begin{equation} \mathrm{RHom}(f_*{\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{G}}) \cong \mathrm{RHom}({\mathscr{F}},f^!{\mathscr{G}}), \end{equation} where $f^!$ is the twisted pullback functor (if ${\mathscr{G}}$ is perfect, $f^!{\mathscr{G}} \cong {\mathscr{G}} \otimes \omega^\bullet_{X/Y}$, where $\omega^\bullet_{X/Y} = f^!{\mathscr{O}}_Y$ is the relative dualizing complex). In other words, the twisted pullback functor is right adjoint to the (derived) pushforward.
nodes.name: Grothendieck duality
nodes.statement_short: For proper f, RHom(f_*F, G) = RHom(F, f^!G): the twisted pullback is right adjoint to pushforward.
assumptions: $f \colon X \to Y$ be a proper morphism
conclusions: the twisted pullback functor is right adjoint to the (derived) pushforward

nodes.statement: \mathrm{RHom}(f_*{\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{G}}) \cong \mathrm{RHom}({\mathscr{F}},f^!{\mathscr{G}}),
nodes.name: Equation (3) Gd
nodes.label: eq:Gd

nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a projective Gorenstein ${\mathsf{k}}$-scheme of dimension $n$. If either ${\mathscr{F}}$ or ${\mathscr{G}}$ is a perfect complex, there is a natural Serre duality isomorphism \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Ext}^i({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{G}})^\vee \cong \mathrm{Ext}^{n-i}({\mathscr{G}},{\mathscr{F}} \otimes \omega_X). \end{equation*}
nodes.name: Serre duality for Gorenstein schemes
nodes.statement_short: Serre duality Ext^i(F,G)^dual = Ext^{n-i}(G, F tensor omega_X) on a projective Gorenstein scheme when F or G is perfect.
assumptions: $X$ be a projective Gorenstein ${\mathsf{k}}$-scheme of dimension $n$
either ${\mathscr{F}}$ or ${\mathscr{G}}$ is a perfect complex
conclusions: there is a natural Serre duality isomorphism
nodes.label: proposition:serre-gorenstein

nodes.statement: Let $f \colon X \to \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}})$ be the structure morphism. If ${\mathscr{F}}$ is a locally free sheaf, then we have $\mathrm{Ext}^i({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{G}}) \cong H^i(X,{\mathscr{F}}^\vee \otimes {\mathscr{G}})$, and this is a cohomology group of $f_*({\mathscr{F}}^\vee \otimes {\mathscr{G}})$. By Grothendieck duality \begin{equation*} \mathrm{RHom}(f_*({\mathscr{F}}^\vee \otimes {\mathscr{G}}),{\mathsf{k}}) \cong \mathrm{RHom}({\mathscr{F}}^\vee \otimes {\mathscr{G}},f^!({\mathsf{k}})). \end{equation*} Since $X$ is Gorenstein, $f^!({\mathsf{k}}) \cong \omega_X[n]$, hence the right hand side equals $\mathrm{RHom}({\mathscr{F}}^\vee \otimes {\mathscr{G}}, \omega_X[n])$. Since~${\mathscr{F}}$ is locally free, this can be rewritten as $\mathrm{RHom}({\mathscr{G}},{\mathscr{F}} \otimes \omega_X[n])$. Computing the cohomology groups in degree $-i$, we deduce the required duality isomorphism. For arbitrary perfect ${\mathscr{F}}$ the Serre duality follows by using the stupid filtration. Finally, when ${\mathscr{G}}$ is perfect, we replace ${\mathscr{F}}$ by ${\mathscr{G}}$, ${\mathscr{G}}$ by ${\mathscr{F}} \otimes \omega_X$, and $i$ by $n - i$, and deduce the required isomorphism from the previous case.
nodes.statement_short: Grothendieck duality for the structure morphism, first for locally free F, then by filtrations.
nodes.name: Proof of Serre duality for Gorenstein schemes
Structure morphism; reduce Ext to cohomology for locally free F
nodes.statement: Let $f \colon X \to \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}})$ be the structure morphism. If ${\mathscr{F}}$ is a locally free sheaf, then we have $\mathrm{Ext}^i({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{G}}) \cong H^i(X,{\mathscr{F}}^\vee \otimes {\mathscr{G}})$, and this is a cohomology group of $f_*({\mathscr{F}}^\vee \otimes {\mathscr{G}})$.
nodes.statement_short: Structure morphism; reduce Ext to cohomology for locally free F

nodes.name: Apply Grothendieck duality and Gorenstein dualizing complex
nodes.statement: By Grothendieck duality \begin{equation*} \mathrm{RHom}(f_*({\mathscr{F}}^\vee \otimes {\mathscr{G}}),{\mathsf{k}}) \cong \mathrm{RHom}({\mathscr{F}}^\vee \otimes {\mathscr{G}},f^!({\mathsf{k}})). \end{equation*} Since $X$ is Gorenstein, $f^!({\mathsf{k}}) \cong \omega_X[n]$, hence the right hand side equals $\mathrm{RHom}({\mathscr{F}}^\vee \otimes {\mathscr{G}}, \omega_X[n])$. Since~${\mathscr{F}}$ is locally free, this can be rewritten as $\mathrm{RHom}({\mathscr{G}},{\mathscr{F}} \otimes \omega_X[n])$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Grothendieck duality and Gorenstein dualizing complex

nodes.name: Read off the duality in the locally free case
nodes.statement: Computing the cohomology groups in degree $-i$, we deduce the required duality isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Read off the duality in the locally free case

nodes.name: Extend to perfect F by the stupid filtration
nodes.statement: For arbitrary perfect ${\mathscr{F}}$ the Serre duality follows by using the stupid filtration.
nodes.statement_short: Extend to perfect F by the stupid filtration

nodes.name: Symmetric case by swapping roles
nodes.statement: Finally, when ${\mathscr{G}}$ is perfect, we replace ${\mathscr{F}}$ by ${\mathscr{G}}$, ${\mathscr{G}}$ by ${\mathscr{F}} \otimes \omega_X$, and $i$ by $n - i$, and deduce the required isomorphism from the previous case.
nodes.statement_short: Symmetric case by swapping roles

nodes.statement: It follows from sheafified Grothendieck duality that \begin{equation*} \mathrm{R}\mathscr{H}\mathit{om}(-,\omega^\bullet_{X/{\mathsf{k}}}) \colon {\mathbf{D}}(X)^{\mathrm{opp}} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } {\mathbf{D}}(X). \end{equation*} is an equivalence of categories.
nodes.name: Grothendieck duality functor is an anti-equivalence
conclusions: is an equivalence of categories

nodes.statement: In case when the scheme $X$ is Gorenstein, the dualizing complex $\omega^\bullet_{X/{\mathsf{k}}}$ is a shift of the canonical line bundle, $\omega^\bullet_{X/{\mathsf{k}}} \cong \omega_X[\dim X]$, and it follows that the usual duality functor \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{F}} \mapsto {\mathscr{F}}^\vee := \mathrm{R}\mathscr{H}\mathit{om}({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{O}}_X) \cong \mathrm{R}\mathscr{H}\mathit{om}({\mathscr{F}},\omega_X^\bullet) \otimes \omega_X^{-1}[-\dim X] \end{equation*} is also an equivalence of categories ${\mathbf{D}}(X)^{\mathrm{opp}} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } {\mathbf{D}}(X)$.
nodes.name: Derived dual F^v on a Gorenstein scheme
nodes.statement_short: On a Gorenstein scheme the derived dual F^v = RHom(F,O_X) is an anti-autoequivalence of D(X).

nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a sextic du Val del Pezzo surface over an algebraically closed field ${\mathsf{k}}$ and let~$\pi \colon {\widetilde{X}} \to X$ be its minimal resolution of singularities. There is a semiorthogonal decomposition \begin{equation} {\mathbf{D}}({\widetilde{X}}) = \langle {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1, {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2, {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3 \rangle, \end{equation} whose components are generated by the following exceptional collections of line bundles \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1 &= \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}} \rangle,\\ {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2 &= \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1), {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_2), {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_3) \rangle,\\ {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3 &= \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h), {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3) \rangle. \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.name: Exceptional collection on the resolution of a sextic del Pezzo surface
nodes.statement_short: D(X~) has a three-block semiorthogonal decomposition generated by exceptional line bundles O, O(h-e_i), O(h), O(2h-e1-e2-e3).
assumptions: $X$ be a sextic du Val del Pezzo surface over an algebraically closed field ${\mathsf{k}}$
$\pi \colon {\widetilde{X}} \to X$ be its minimal resolution of singularities
conclusions: There is a semiorthogonal decomposition
nodes.label: proposition:tx-excol

nodes.statement: {\mathbf{D}}({\widetilde{X}}) = \langle {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1, {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2, {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3 \rangle,
nodes.name: Equation (4) dbtx
nodes.label: eq:dbtx

nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1 &= \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}} \rangle,\\ {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2 &= \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1), {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_2), {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_3) \rangle,\\ {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3 &= \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h), {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3) \rangle. \end{aligned}
nodes.name: Equation (5) tx-excol
nodes.label: eq:tx-excol

nodes.statement: {\mathbf{D}}({\widetilde{X}}) = \langle {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3^\vee, {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2^\vee, {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1^\vee \rangle.
nodes.name: Equation (6) dbtx-dual
nodes.label: eq:dbtx-dual

nodes.statement: Below we denote by ${\mathbb{L}}_{\mathcal{A}}$ the left mutation functor through an admissible subcategory ${\mathcal{A}}$.
nodes.name: Left mutation functor

nodes.statement: The semiorthogonal decomposition~\eqref{eq:dbtx-dual} is right mutation-dual to~\eqref{eq:dbtx}, i.e., \begin{equation*} {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1^\vee = {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1, \qquad {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2^\vee = {\mathbb{L}}_{{\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1}({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2), \quad\text{and}\quad {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3^\vee = {\mathbb{L}}_{{\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1}({\mathbb{L}}_{{\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2}({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3)) = {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3 \otimes \omega_{\widetilde{X}}. \end{equation*}
nodes.name: Self-duality of the decomposition of D(X~)
nodes.statement_short: The dual decomposition of D(X~) is obtained from the original one by right mutation-duality.
conclusions: The semiorthogonal decomposition~\eqref{eq:dbtx-dual} is right mutation-dual to~\eqref{eq:dbtx}
nodes.label: lemma:dual-sod-tx

nodes.statement: The claim is trivial for the first component, since ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1^\vee = \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}^\vee \rangle = \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}} \rangle = {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1$, and is easy for the last component, since ${\mathbb{L}}_{{\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1}({\mathbb{L}}_{{\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2}({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3)) = {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3 \otimes \omega_{\widetilde{X}}$ and \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h) \otimes \omega_{\widetilde{X}} && \cong {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(-2h + e_1 + e_2 + e_3) && \cong {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)^\vee,\\ & {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3) \otimes \omega_{\widetilde{X}} && \cong {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(-h) && \cong {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h)^\vee. \end{aligned} \end{equation} Finally, for the second component we have ${\mathbb{L}}_{{\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1}({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2) = {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1^\perp \cap {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3^\perp = ({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1^\vee)^\perp \cap {}^\perp({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3 \otimes \omega_X) = {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2^\vee$ by Serre duality.
nodes.statement_short: Direct check on each component using Serre duality.
nodes.name: Proof of Self-duality of the decomposition of D(X~)

nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} & {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h) \otimes \omega_{\widetilde{X}} && \cong {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(-2h + e_1 + e_2 + e_3) && \cong {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)^\vee,\\ & {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3) \otimes \omega_{\widetilde{X}} && \cong {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(-h) && \cong {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h)^\vee. \end{aligned}
nodes.name: Equation (7) ce3-dual
nodes.label: eq:ce3-dual

nodes.statement: For $m = 2$ and $m = 3$ we denote by ${\tilde{R}}_m$ the Auslander algebra defined by~\eqref{eq:trm}, and refer to Appendix~\ref{appendix:auslander} for its basic properties, especially note the definition~\eqref{eq:projective-resolution-ei} of the {\sf standard exceptional modules} and Proposition~\ref{proposition:rm-equivalence}.
nodes.name: Auslander algebra R~_m (notation)

nodes.statement: The components ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i$ of~\eqref{eq:dbtx} are equivalent to products of derived categories of Auslander algebras as indicated in the next table: \begin{equation*} \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Type of $X$} & {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1 & {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2 & {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3 \\ \hline 0 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \\ \hline 1 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_2) \\ \hline 2 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_2) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \\ \hline 3 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_2) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_2) \\ \hline 4 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_3) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \\ \hline 5 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_3) & {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_2) \\ \hline \end{array} \end{equation*} This equivalence takes the exceptional line bundles in~\eqref{eq:tx-excol} to the standard exceptional modules over the corresponding Auslander algebra.
nodes.name: Components of D(X~) as derived categories of Auslander algebras
nodes.statement_short: Each component of the decomposition of D(X~) is a product of D(k), D(R~_2), D(R~_3) according to the type of X.
conclusions: The components ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i$ of~\eqref{eq:dbtx} are equivalent to products of derived categories of Auslander algebras as indicated in the next table
nodes.label: proposition:tcai-auslander

nodes.statement: The component ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1$ is generated by a single exceptional object, hence is equivalent to ${\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}})$. So, in view of Proposition~\ref{proposition:rm-equivalence} to prove the proposition it is enough to compute $\mathrm{Ext}$-spaces between the exceptional line bundles forming the components ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2$ and ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3$ of the semiorthogonal decomposition~\eqref{eq:dbtx}. First of all, we have \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Ext}^p({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_i), {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_j)) \cong H^p({\widetilde{X}}, {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(e_i - e_j)). \end{equation*} Assuming $i \ne j$ and using exact sequences (note that $e_i\cdot e_j = 0$ and $e_i^2 = -1$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma:pic-tx}) \begin{equation*} 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(e_i - e_j) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(e_i) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{E_j} \to 0, \qquad\qquad 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}} \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(e_i) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{E_i}(-1) \to 0, \end{equation*} we obtain an exact sequence \begin{equation*} 0 \to H^0({\widetilde{X}}, {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(e_i - e_j)) \to {\mathsf{k}} \to {\mathsf{k}} \to H^1({\widetilde{X}}, {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(e_i - e_j)) \to 0, \end{equation*} where the middle map is given by the restriction to $E_j$ of the equation of $E_i$. This restriction vanishes if and only if $E_j$ is a component of $E_i$ --- in this case we deduce that $\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_i), {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_j)) \cong {\mathsf{k}} \oplus {\mathsf{k}}[-1]$, and otherwise $\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_i), {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_j)) = 0$. By Proposition~\ref{proposition:rm-equivalence} this gives the required description of ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2$ in types from~0 to 3. In the last two types (4 and 5) it remains to check that multiplication map \begin{equation} \mathrm{Ext}^p({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_1),{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_2)) \otimes \mathrm{Ext}^q({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_2),{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_3)) \to \mathrm{Ext}^{p+q}({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_1),{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_3)) \end{equation} is an isomorphism when $p = 0$ or $q = 0$. For this consider exact sequences \begin{equation} 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1) \xrightarrow{\ \Delta_{12}\ } {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_2) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{12}}(-1) \to 0, \end{equation} \begin{equation} 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_2) \xrightarrow{\ \Delta_{23}\ } {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_3) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{23}}(-1) \to 0, \end{equation} where $\Delta_{12} = E_1 - E_2$ and $\Delta_{23} = E_2 - E_3$. Using Lemma~\ref{lemma:pic-tx}, we compute \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_1),{\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{23}}(-1)) \cong H^\bullet(\Delta_{23},{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(e_1 - h)\vert_{\Delta_{23}} \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{23}}(-1)) = H^\bullet(\Delta_{23},{\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{23}}(-1)) = 0. \end{equation*} Applying the functor $\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_1),-)$ to~\eqref{eq:e23}, we deduce that~\eqref{eq:multiplication-ext-tx} is an isomorphism for~$q = 0$. Similarly, by Serre duality $\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{12}}(-1),{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_3))$ is dual to $\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(e_1 + e_2 - 2h),{\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{12}}(-1))$, and a computation similar to the above shows it is zero. Applying the functor $\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet(-,{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_3))$ to~\eqref{eq:e12}, we deduce that~~\eqref{eq:multiplication-ext-tx} is an isomorphism for $p = 0$. To describe ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3$ we only need to compute \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Ext}^p({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h), {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)) \cong H^p({\widetilde{X}}, {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)). \end{equation*} Using exact sequences \begin{align*} 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h) &\to {\mathscr{O}}_{E_1} \to 0,\\ 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1 - e_2) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1) &\to {\mathscr{O}}_{E_2} \to 0,\\ 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1 - e_2) &\to {\mathscr{O}}_{E_3} \to 0, \end{align*} we conclude that $H^\bullet({\widetilde{X}}, {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)) = 0$ if the three centers of the blowups are not contained on a line (i.e., in types~0, 2, and 4), and $H^0({\widetilde{X}}, {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)) = H^1({\widetilde{X}}, {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)) = {\mathsf{k}}$ otherwise. By Proposition~\ref{proposition:rm-equivalence} this describes ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce via Proposition rm-equivalence to computing Ext-spaces between the exceptional line bundles, using blowup exact sequences.
nodes.name: Proof of Components of D(X~) as derived categories of Auslander algebras
Reduce to Ext computations via the Auslander characterization

nodes.statement_short: Compute that cohomology via restriction to E_j

nodes.name: Conclude for A~_2 in types 0-3
nodes.statement: By Proposition~\ref{proposition:rm-equivalence} this gives the required description of ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2$ in types from~0 to 3.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude for A~_2 in types 0-3

nodes.name: Types 4,5: check the multiplication map using sequences (e12),(e23)
nodes.statement: In the last two types (4 and 5) it remains to check that multiplication map \begin{equation} \mathrm{Ext}^p({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_1),{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_2)) \otimes \mathrm{Ext}^q({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_2),{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_3)) \to \mathrm{Ext}^{p+q}({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_1),{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_3)) \end{equation} is an isomorphism when $p = 0$ or $q = 0$. For this consider exact sequences \begin{equation} 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1) \xrightarrow{\ \Delta_{12}\ } {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_2) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{12}}(-1) \to 0, \end{equation} \begin{equation} 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_2) \xrightarrow{\ \Delta_{23}\ } {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_3) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{23}}(-1) \to 0, \end{equation} where $\Delta_{12} = E_1 - E_2$ and $\Delta_{23} = E_2 - E_3$.
nodes.statement_short: Types 4,5: check the multiplication map using sequences (e12),(e23)

nodes.statement: \mathrm{Ext}^p({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_1),{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_2)) \otimes \mathrm{Ext}^q({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_2),{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_3)) \to \mathrm{Ext}^{p+q}({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_1),{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_3))
nodes.name: Equation (8) multiplication-ext-tx
nodes.label: eq:multiplication-ext-tx

nodes.statement: 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1) \xrightarrow{\ \Delta_{12}\ } {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_2) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{12}}(-1) \to 0,
nodes.name: Equation (9) e12
nodes.label: eq:e12

nodes.statement: 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_2) \xrightarrow{\ \Delta_{23}\ } {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_3) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{23}}(-1) \to 0,
nodes.name: Equation (10) e23
nodes.label: eq:e23

nodes.name: Isomorphism for q = 0
nodes.statement: Using Lemma~\ref{lemma:pic-tx}, we compute \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_1),{\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{23}}(-1)) \cong H^\bullet(\Delta_{23},{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(e_1 - h)\vert_{\Delta_{23}} \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{23}}(-1)) = H^\bullet(\Delta_{23},{\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{23}}(-1)) = 0. \end{equation*} Applying the functor $\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_1),-)$ to~\eqref{eq:e23}, we deduce that~\eqref{eq:multiplication-ext-tx} is an isomorphism for~$q = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Isomorphism for q = 0

nodes.name: Isomorphism for p = 0 via Serre duality
nodes.statement: Similarly, by Serre duality $\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{12}}(-1),{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_3))$ is dual to $\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(e_1 + e_2 - 2h),{\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{12}}(-1))$, and a computation similar to the above shows it is zero. Applying the functor $\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet(-,{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_3))$ to~\eqref{eq:e12}, we deduce that~~\eqref{eq:multiplication-ext-tx} is an isomorphism for $p = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Isomorphism for p = 0 via Serre duality

nodes.name: Reduce A~_3 to cohomology of O(h-e1-e2-e3)
nodes.statement: To describe ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3$ we only need to compute \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Ext}^p({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h), {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)) \cong H^p({\widetilde{X}}, {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Reduce A~_3 to cohomology of O(h-e1-e2-e3)

nodes.name: Compute this cohomology by type
nodes.statement: Using exact sequences \begin{align*} 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h) &\to {\mathscr{O}}_{E_1} \to 0,\\ 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1 - e_2) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1) &\to {\mathscr{O}}_{E_2} \to 0,\\ 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1 - e_2) &\to {\mathscr{O}}_{E_3} \to 0, \end{align*} we conclude that $H^\bullet({\widetilde{X}}, {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)) = 0$ if the three centers of the blowups are not contained on a line (i.e., in types~0, 2, and 4), and $H^0({\widetilde{X}}, {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)) = H^1({\widetilde{X}}, {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)) = {\mathsf{k}}$ otherwise.
nodes.statement_short: Compute this cohomology by type

nodes.name: Conclude for A~_3
nodes.statement: By Proposition~\ref{proposition:rm-equivalence} this describes ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude for A~_3

nodes.statement: The nontrivial morphisms between the line bundles ${\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_1)$, ${\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_2)$, and ${\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_3)$ when exist are realized by exact sequences~\eqref{eq:e12} and~\eqref{eq:e23}. Analogously, the nontrivial morphism between the line bundles ${\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h)$ and ${\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)$ is realized by the exact sequence \begin{equation} 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h) \xrightarrow{\ \Delta_{123}\ } {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{123}}(-1) \to 0. \end{equation} This shows that each category ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i$ is a product of categories of the form described in~\cite[Theorem~2.5]{hille2017tilting}, and in fact, the Auslander algebras ${\tilde{R}}_m$ appearing in Proposition~\ref{proposition:tcai-auslander}, are nothing but the particular forms of the algebras from \emph{loc.\ cit.}, cf.~\cite[\S3.2]{hille2017tilting}.
nodes.name: Relation to Hille-Ploog tilting chains
nodes.statement_short: Nontrivial morphisms come from sequences (e12),(e23),(e123), so the components are products of Hille-Ploog categories.

nodes.statement: 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h) \xrightarrow{\ \Delta_{123}\ } {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{123}}(-1) \to 0.
nodes.name: Equation (11) e123
nodes.label: eq:e123

nodes.statement: Comparing exact sequences~\eqref{eq:resolution-simple} of standard exceptional modules over an Auslander algebra with the exact sequences~\eqref{eq:e12}, \eqref{eq:e23} and~\eqref{eq:e123}, and taking into account that the equivalence of Proposition~\ref{proposition:tcai-auslander} takes the exceptional line bundles generating ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i$ to the standard exceptional modules over the corresponding Auslander algebras, we conclude that the sheaves~${\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1)$ go to the corresponding simple modules. For instance, for a surface of type 5, when we have the maximal number of $(-2)$-curves on ${\widetilde{X}}$, and when ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2 \cong {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_3)$, ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3 \cong {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_2)$, the sheaves ${\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{12}}(-1)$ and~${\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{23}}(-1)$ go to $S_1$ and $S_2$ in ${\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_3)$, and the sheaf ${\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{123}}(-1)$ goes to $S_1$ in ${\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_2)$.
nodes.name: (-2)-curve sheaves correspond to simple modules
nodes.statement_short: Under the Auslander-algebra equivalences the sheaves O_Delta(-1) go to simple modules.
nodes.label: remark:delta-simples

nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a sextic du Val del Pezzo surface over an algebraically closed field~${\mathsf{k}}$, and let $\pi \colon {\widetilde{X}} \to X$ be its minimal resolution of singularities. Then there is a unique semiorthogonal decomposition \begin{equation} {\mathbf{D}}(X) = \langle {\mathcal{A}}_1, {\mathcal{A}}_2, {\mathcal{A}}_3 \rangle, \end{equation} such that $\pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i) = {\mathcal{A}}_i$ and $\pi^*({\mathcal{A}}_i \cap {\mathbf{D}}^{\mathrm{perf}}(X)) \subset {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i$, where ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i$ are the components of~\eqref{eq:dbtx}. The components~${\mathcal{A}}_i$ are admissible with projection functors of finite cohomological amplitude, and are equivalent to products of derived categories of finite-dimensional algebras as indicated in the next table: \begin{equation*} \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Type of $X$} & {\mathcal{A}}_1 & {\mathcal{A}}_2 & {\mathcal{A}}_3 \\ \hline 0 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \\ \hline 1 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^2) \\ \hline 2 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^2) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \\ \hline 3 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^2) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^2) \\ \hline 4 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^3) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \\ \hline 5 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^3) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^2) \\ \hline \end{array} \end{equation*} The categories ${\mathcal{A}}_i^{\mathrm{perf}} := {\mathcal{A}}_i \cap {\mathbf{D}}^{\mathrm{perf}}(X)$ form a semiorthogonal decomposition of the perfect category \begin{equation*} {\mathbf{D}}^{\mathrm{perf}}(X) = \langle {\mathcal{A}}_1^{\mathrm{perf}}, {\mathcal{A}}_2^{\mathrm{perf}}, {\mathcal{A}}_3^{\mathrm{perf}} \rangle. \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 3.2 Semiorthogonal decomposition for a sextic del Pezzo surface
nodes.name: Semiorthogonal decomposition of a sextic du Val del Pezzo surface
nodes.statement_short: D(X) has a unique decomposition <A1,A2,A3> pushed forward from D(X~), with components products of D(k[t]/t^m) by type.

Therefore, by~\cite[Proposition~4.2]{kuznetsov2011base} it extends to a semiorthogonal decomposition of the bounded above derived category \begin{equation} {\mathbf{D}}^-({\widetilde{X}}) = \langle {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1^-, {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2^-, {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3^- \rangle. \end{equation}

conclusions: there is a canonical direct sum decomposition
nodes.label: lemma:ker-pis

nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lemma:pi-properties} an object ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathbf{D}}^-({\widetilde{X}})$ is in $\mathrm{Ker}\pi_*$ if and only if every its cohomology sheaf~${\mathscr{H}}^j({\mathscr{F}})$ is an iterated extension of sheaves ${\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1)$ where $\Delta$ run over the set ${\boldsymbol\Delta}$ of all $(-2)$-curves on~${\widetilde{X}}$. Note that ${\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1) \in {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2$ for $\Delta \in {\boldsymbol\Delta}_2$ by~\eqref{eq:e12} and~\eqref{eq:e23}, while ${\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1) \in {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3$ for $\Delta \in {\boldsymbol\Delta}_3$ by~\eqref{eq:e123}. Moreover, the subcategories generated by the sheaves ${\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1)$ with $\Delta \in {\boldsymbol\Delta}_2$ and $\Delta \in {\boldsymbol\Delta}_3$ are completely orthogonal, since the supports of these sheaves do not intersect. This last observation shows that any ${\mathscr{F}} \in \mathrm{Ker}\pi_*$ decomposes as ${\mathscr{F}}_2 \oplus {\mathscr{F}}_3$ with the required properties (just take ${\mathscr{F}}_2$ and ${\mathscr{F}}_3$ to be the components of ${\mathscr{F}}$ supported on the union of the curves $\Delta$ from ${\boldsymbol\Delta}_2$ and ${\boldsymbol\Delta}_3$ respectively).

nodes.statement_short: Kernel of pi_* is generated by O_Delta(-1), which lie in the appropriate components and have disjoint supports.

conclusions: We have $\mathrm{Hom}({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i^-,{\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_j^- \cap \mathrm{Ker} \pi_*) = 0$ for any $i \ne j$

nodes.statement: Since ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i^-$ is generated by an exceptional collection of line bundles and ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_j^- \cap \mathrm{Ker} \pi_*$ is generated by sheaves ${\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1)$ for $\Delta \in {\boldsymbol\Delta}_j$, it is enough to check that any of the line bundles generating ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i^-$ restricts trivially to any curve $\Delta$ from ${\boldsymbol\Delta}_j$. For $i = 1$ this is evident; for $i = 2$ we have $(h-e_k)\cdot \Delta_{123} = (h - e_k)(h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3) = 1 - 1 = 0$, and for $i = 3$ we have $h\cdot (e_k - e_l) = 0$ and $(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3) \cdot (e_k - e_l) = 1 - 1 = 0$.

nodes.statement: The subcategories ${\mathcal{A}}_i^- = \{ {\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathbf{D}}^-(X) \mid \pi^*({\mathscr{F}}) \in {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i^- \} \subset {\mathbf{D}}^-(X)$ form a semiorthogonal decomposition \begin{equation*} {\mathbf{D}}^-(X) = \langle {\mathcal{A}}_1^-, {\mathcal{A}}_2^-, {\mathcal{A}}_3^- \rangle \end{equation*} with projection functors given by \begin{equation} \alpha_i = \pi_* \circ \tilde\alpha_i \circ \pi^*. \end{equation} Moreover, we have \begin{equation} \pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i^-) = {\mathcal{A}}_i^-. \end{equation}

nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lemma:pi-properties} the functor $\pi^* \colon {\mathbf{D}}^-(X) \to {\mathbf{D}}^-({\widetilde{X}})$ is fully faithful, hence the subcategories ${\mathcal{A}}_i^-$ are semiorthogonal. Let us prove~\eqref{eq:pis-ai}. For this take any object ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i^-$ and consider the standard triangle \begin{equation*} \pi^*(\pi_*{\mathscr{F}}) \to {\mathscr{F}} \to {\mathscr{G}}. \end{equation*} Then, of course, ${\mathscr{G}} \in \mathrm{Ker}\pi_*$. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:ker-pis} we have ${\mathscr{G}} = {\mathscr{G}}_2 \oplus {\mathscr{G}}_3$ with~${\mathscr{G}}_j \in {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_j^- \cap \mathrm{Ker} \pi_*$. If~$j \ne i$ then~$\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{G}}_j) = 0$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma:ker-pis-orthogonality} and $\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet(\pi^*(\pi_*{\mathscr{F}}),{\mathscr{G}}_j) = 0$ since ${\mathscr{G}}_j \in \mathrm{Ker} \pi_*$. It follows from the above triangle that $\mathrm{Hom}({\mathscr{G}},{\mathscr{G}}_j) = 0$, hence ${\mathscr{G}}_j = 0$ since it is a direct summand of ${\mathscr{G}}$. Therefore we have ${\mathscr{G}} \in {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i^-$, hence $\pi^*(\pi_*{\mathscr{F}}) \in {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i^-$, hence $\pi_*{\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathcal{A}}_i^-$ by definition of the latter. This proves an inclusion $\pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i^-) \subset {\mathcal{A}}_i^-$. The other inclusion follows from~\eqref{eq:pis-pis-id}. Now let us decompose any ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathbf{D}}^-(X)$. For this take ${\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}} := \pi^*({\mathscr{F}}) \in {\mathbf{D}}^-({\widetilde{X}})$ and consider its decomposition with respect to~\eqref{eq:dbtx-}. It is given by a chain of morphisms \begin{equation*} 0 = {\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}_3 \rightarrow {\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}_2 \rightarrow {\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}_1 \rightarrow {\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}_0 = {\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}, \end{equation*} whose cones are $\tilde\alpha_i({\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}) \in {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i^-$. Pushing it forward to $X$, we obtain a chain of morphisms \begin{equation*} 0 = \pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}_3) \rightarrow \pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}_2) \rightarrow \pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}_1) \rightarrow \pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}_0) = \pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}) \cong {\mathscr{F}}, \end{equation*} whose cones are $\pi_*(\tilde\alpha_i({\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}})) \cong \pi_*(\tilde\alpha_i(\pi^*{\mathscr{F}})) \in \pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i^-) = {\mathcal{A}}_i^-$. This proves the semiorthogonal decomposition and shows that its projection functors are given by~\eqref{eq:alpha}.

nodes.statement: For the first claim it is enough to check that the projection functors $\alpha_i$ preserve boundedness. Take any ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathbf{D}}^{[a,b]}(X)$ and consider $\pi^*({\mathscr{F}}) \in {\mathbf{D}}^{(-\infty,b]}({\widetilde{X}})$. By projection formula $\pi_*(\pi^*({\mathscr{F}})) \cong {\mathscr{F}}$, hence by Lemma~\ref{lemma:spectral} we have $\tau^{\le a-1}(\pi^*({\mathscr{F}})) \in \mathrm{Ker} \pi_*$. Consider the triangle \begin{equation*} \tilde\alpha_i(\tau^{\le a-1}(\pi^*({\mathscr{F}}))) \to \tilde\alpha_i(\pi^*({\mathscr{F}})) \to \tilde\alpha_i(\tau^{\ge a}(\pi^*({\mathscr{F}}))) \end{equation*} obtained by applying the projection functor $\tilde\alpha_i$ to the canonical truncation triangle. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:ker-pis} the functor $\tilde\alpha_i$ preserves~$\mathrm{Ker}\pi_*$, hence the first term of the triangle is in $\mathrm{Ker} \pi_*$. Therefore, applying the pushforward we obtain an isomorphism \begin{equation*} \alpha_i({\mathscr{F}}) = \pi_*(\tilde\alpha_i(\pi^*({\mathscr{F}}))) \cong \pi_*(\tilde\alpha_i(\tau^{\ge a}(\pi^*({\mathscr{F}}))). \end{equation*} So, it remains to note that $\tau^{\ge a}(\pi^*({\mathscr{F}})) \in {\mathbf{D}}^{[a,b]}({\widetilde{X}})$, hence $\pi_*(\tilde\alpha_i(\tau^{\ge a}(\pi^*({\mathscr{F}})))$ is bounded, since both $\tilde\alpha_i$ and $\pi_*$ preserve boundedness. Moreover, if the cohomological amplitude of $\tilde\alpha_i$ is $(p,q)$ (it is finite since~${\widetilde{X}}$ is smooth, see~\cite[Proposition~2.5]{kuznetsov2008resolution}), then $\pi_*(\tilde\alpha_i(\tau^{\ge a}(\pi^*({\mathscr{F}}))) \in {\mathbf{D}}^{[a+p,b+q+1]}(X)$. In particular, $\alpha_i$ has finite cohomological amplitude. Let us prove the last claim. By~\eqref{eq:pis-ai} we have $\pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i) \subset {\mathcal{A}}_i^-$, and since $\pi_*$ preserves boundedness, we have $\pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i) \subset {\mathcal{A}}_i$. To check that this inclusion is an equality, take any ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathcal{A}}_i$. By Corollary~\ref{corollary:pis-epi} there exists ${\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}} \in {\mathbf{D}}({\widetilde{X}})$ such that ${\mathscr{F}} \cong \pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}})$. Let ${\mathscr{G}}$ be the cone of the natural morphism $\pi^*{\mathscr{F}} \to {\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}$. Then ${\mathscr{G}} \in \mathrm{Ker} \pi_*$. Moreover, $\tilde\alpha_i({\mathscr{G}}) \in \mathrm{Ker} \pi_*$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma:ker-pis}, hence applying the functor $\pi_* \circ \tilde\alpha_i$ to the distinguished triangle $\pi^*{\mathscr{F}} \to {\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}} \to {\mathscr{G}}$, we deduce an isomorphism ${\mathscr{F}} \cong \alpha_i({\mathscr{F}}) \cong \pi_*(\tilde\alpha_i({\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}))$, and it remains to note that $\tilde\alpha_i({\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}) \in {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i$.

nodes.statement: By definition $\gamma \circ \pi_{m*} = \pi_* \circ \tilde\gamma \circ \pi_m^* \circ \pi_{m*}$, so for commutativity of the first diagram it is enough to check that for any $M \in {\mathbf{D}}^-({\tilde{R}}_m)$ the cone of the canonical morphism $\pi_m^*(\pi_{m*}M) \to M$ is killed by the functor $\pi_* \circ \tilde\gamma$. But this cone, by Proposition~\ref{proposition:auslander-localization} is contained in the subcategory generated by the simple modules $S_1,\dots,S_{m-1}$ over ${\tilde{R}}_m$. By Remark~\ref{remark:delta-simples} the functor $\tilde\gamma$ takes these modules to sheaves ${\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1)$ for appropriate $(-2)$-curves $\Delta$ on ${\widetilde{X}}$, and the functor $\pi_*$ kills every ${\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1)$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma:pi-properties}. For commutativity of the second diagram note that by Proposition~\ref{proposition:auslander-localization} the image of the functor~$\pi_m^*$ is the left orthogonal ${}^\perp\langle S_1,\dots, S_{m-1} \rangle \subset {\mathbf{D}}^-({\tilde{R}}_m)$ of the subcategory generated by the simple modules. Therefore, using Lemma~\ref{lemma:ker-pis-orthogonality} and Remark~\ref{remark:delta-simples} we deduce that the image of $\tilde\gamma \circ \pi_m^*$ is contained in the left orthogonal ${}^\perp \langle {\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1) \rangle \subset {\mathbf{D}}^-({\widetilde{X}})$ of the subcategory generated by all $(-2)$-curves $\Delta$. Hence, by Lemma~\ref{lemma:pi-properties} it is contained in the image of $\pi^* \colon {\mathbf{D}}^-(X) \to {\mathbf{D}}^-({\widetilde{X}})$. Thus, the functor $\pi^* \circ \pi_*$ is identical on the image of $\tilde\gamma \circ \pi_m^*$, hence $\tilde\gamma \circ \pi_m^* \cong \pi^* \circ \pi_* \circ \tilde\gamma \circ \pi_m^* \cong \pi^* \circ \gamma$, and so the second diagram commutes. Let us show that $\gamma$ is fully faithful. Indeed, by commutativity of the second diagram in~\eqref{eq:gamma-tgamma}, this follows from full faithfulness of the functors $\pi_m^*$ (Proposition~\ref{proposition:auslander-localization}), $\tilde\gamma$ (Proposition~\ref{proposition:tcai-auslander}), and $\pi^*$ (Lemma~\ref{lemma:pi-properties}). Finally, let us show that $\gamma$ preserves boundedness. Indeed, take any $N \in {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m)$. By Proposition~\ref{proposition:auslander-localization} there exists $M \in {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_m)$ such that $N \cong \pi_{m*}(M)$. Then $\gamma(N) = \gamma(\pi_{m*}(M))$ and by commutativity of the first diagram this is the same as $\pi_*(\tilde\gamma(M))$. We know that $\tilde\gamma(M)$ is bounded by Proposition~\ref{proposition:tcai-auslander}, hence so is $\pi_*(\tilde\gamma(M)) = \gamma(N)$.

Moreover, since $\gamma_j$ preserves boundedness, it actually is in ${\mathcal{A}}_i$. nodes.statement: Consider the semiorthogonal decompositions \begin{equation*} {\mathbf{D}}({\widetilde{X}}) = \langle {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3 \otimes \omega_{\widetilde{X}}, {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1, {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2 \rangle \qquad\text{and}\qquad {\mathbf{D}}({\widetilde{X}}) = \langle {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2 \otimes \omega_{\widetilde{X}}, {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3 \otimes \omega_{\widetilde{X}}, {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1 \rangle, \end{equation*} obtained from~\eqref{eq:dbtx} by mutations. Since $\omega_{\widetilde{X}} \cong \pi^*\omega_X$ and $\omega_X$ is a line bundle on $X$, we have \begin{equation*} \pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i \otimes \omega_{\widetilde{X}}) = \pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i) \otimes \omega_X = {\mathcal{A}}_i \otimes \omega_X, \end{equation*} hence the arguments of this subsection also prove semiorthogonal decompositions \begin{equation} {\mathbf{D}}(X) = \langle {\mathcal{A}}_3 \otimes \omega_X, {\mathcal{A}}_1, {\mathcal{A}}_2 \rangle \qquad\text{and}\qquad {\mathbf{D}}(X) = \langle {\mathcal{A}}_2 \otimes \omega_X, {\mathcal{A}}_3 \otimes \omega_X, {\mathcal{A}}_1 \rangle. \end{equation} Since the twist by $\omega_X$ is an autoequivalence of ${\mathbf{D}}(X)$, these decompositions together with~\eqref{eq:dbx} show that each ${\mathcal{A}}_i$ is admissible. Indeed, (up to a twist) each ${\mathcal{A}}_i$ appears in one of the three decompositions on the left, and in one on the right, hence it is both left and right admissible.

nodes.statement: If $X$ is a sextic del Pezzo surface over an algebraically closed field, there is a semiorthogonal decomposition \begin{equation} {\mathbf{D}}(X) = \langle {\mathcal{A}}_3^\vee, {\mathcal{A}}_2^\vee, {\mathcal{A}}_1^\vee \rangle, \end{equation} where \begin{equation*} {\mathcal{A}}_i^\vee := \{ {\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathbf{D}}(X) \mid {\mathscr{F}}^\vee \in {\mathcal{A}}_i \} \cong {\mathbf{D}}(Z_i), \end{equation*} and ${\mathcal{A}}_i$ are the components of~\eqref{eq:dbx}. Moreover, this semiorthogonal decomposition is right mutation-dual to~\eqref{eq:dbx}, i.e., ${\mathcal{A}}_1^\vee = {\mathcal{A}}_1$, ${\mathcal{A}}_2^\vee = {\mathbb{L}}_{{\mathcal{A}}_1}({\mathcal{A}}_2)$ and ${\mathcal{A}}_3^\vee = {\mathbb{L}}_{{\mathcal{A}}_1}({\mathbb{L}}_{{\mathcal{A}}_2}({\mathcal{A}}_3))$.

Since $Z_1$, $Z_2$ and $Z_3$ are themselves Gorenstein, we have ${\mathbf{D}}(Z_i)^{\mathrm{opp}} \cong {\mathbf{D}}(Z_i)$. nodes.statement: Let $Z = \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m)$. For any scheme $Y$ we have an equivalence \begin{equation*} \mathrm{coh}(Y \times Z) \cong \mathrm{coh}(Y,{\mathscr{O}}_Y[t]/t^m), \end{equation*} where the right hand side is the category of coherent sheaves ${\mathscr{F}}$ on $Y$ with an operator $t \colon {\mathscr{F}} \to {\mathscr{F}}$ such that $t^m = 0$. An object $({\mathscr{F}},t) \in \mathrm{coh}(Y,{\mathscr{O}}_Y[t]/t^m)$ considered as a sheaf on $Y \times Z$ is flat over $Z$ if and only if all the maps in the next chain of epimorphisms \begin{equation} \xymatrix@1{{\mathscr{F}}/(t{\mathscr{F}}) \ar@{->>}[r]^-t & (t{\mathscr{F}})/(t^2{\mathscr{F}}) \ar@{->>}[r]^-t & \ \dots\ \ar@{->>}[r]^-t & (t^{m-1}{\mathscr{F}})/(t^m{\mathscr{F}})} \end{equation} are isomorphisms.

nodes.statement: The first part follows immediately from an identification $Y \times Z = \mathrm{Spec}_Y({\mathscr{O}}_Y[t]/t^m)$. To verify flatness, we should compute the derived pullback functors for the embedding $Y \to Y \times Z$ corresponding to the unique closed point of~$Z$. Using the standard resolution \begin{equation*} \dots \xrightarrow{\ t^{m-1}\ } {\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m \xrightarrow{\ t\ } {\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m \xrightarrow{\ t^{m-1}\ } {\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m \xrightarrow{\ t\ } {\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m \xrightarrow{\ \ \ } {\mathsf{k}} \to 0 \end{equation*} we see that $({\mathscr{F}},t)$ is flat over $Z$ if and only if the complex \begin{equation*} \dots \xrightarrow{\ t^{m-1}\ } {\mathscr{F}} \xrightarrow{\ t\ } {\mathscr{F}} \xrightarrow{\ t^{m-1}\ } {\mathscr{F}} \xrightarrow{\ t\ } {\mathscr{F}} \xrightarrow{\ t^{m-1}\ } \dots \end{equation*} is exact. This means that $\mathrm{Ker}({\mathscr{F}} \xrightarrow{\ t\ } {\mathscr{F}}) = t^{m-1}{\mathscr{F}}$ and $\mathrm{Ker}({\mathscr{F}} \xrightarrow{\ t^{m-1}\ } {\mathscr{F}}) = t{\mathscr{F}}$. The second equality implies that the composition of all maps in~\eqref{eq:t-quotients} is an isomorphism, hence so is each of them. On the other hand, if all the maps in~\eqref{eq:t-quotients} are isomorphisms then both equalities above easily follow. This proves the required criterion of flatness.

nodes.statement: First, by commutativity of~\eqref{eq:gamma-tgamma} we have ${\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z \cong \tilde\gamma_Z(\pi_m^*({\mathscr{O}}_Z))$. Furthermore, $\pi_m^*({\mathscr{O}}_Z) \cong P_0$, the principal projective module, see~\eqref{eq:pms}, so that \begin{equation} {\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z \cong \tilde\gamma_Z(P_0). \end{equation} By~\eqref{eq:projective-resolution-ei} the module $P_0$ is an iterated extension of the standard exceptional modules $E_i$, hence $\tilde\gamma_Z(P_0)$ is an iterated extension of $\tilde\gamma_Z(E_i)$, and as it is explained in the proof of Proposition~\ref{proposition:tcai-auslander} these are line bundles on ${\widetilde{X}}$. More precisely, if $Z$ is reduced, then \begin{equation*} {\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z \cong {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_i)\quad\text{for some $i$},\quad\text{or}\quad {\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z \cong {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h),\quad\text{or}\quad {\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z \cong {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h-e_1-e_2-e_3), \end{equation*} depending on whether $Z$ is a component of $Z_2$ or of $Z_3$. Furthermore, if $Z$ has length~2 then we have exact sequences \begin{equation} 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_2) \to {\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_1) \to 0, \end{equation} when $Z$ is a component of $Z_2$, or \begin{equation} 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h-e_1-e_2-e_3) \to {\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h) \to 0, \end{equation} when $Z$ is a component of $Z_3$. Finally, if $Z$ has length~3 we have two exact sequences \begin{equation} 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_3) \to {\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z \to {\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}'_Z \to 0, \qquad\text{where}\qquad 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_2) \to {\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}'_Z \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_1) \to 0. \end{equation} In all cases ${\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z$ is evidently a vector bundle of rank~$\ell(Z)$, and since ${\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z \cong \pi^*{\mathfrak{E}}_Z$, it follows that ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z$ is also a vector bundle of the same rank~$\ell(Z)$. Finally, since $Z \cong \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m)$, the sheaf ${\mathscr{O}}_Z$ is an iterated extension of the sheaf ${\mathscr{O}}_z$, where $z$ is the closed point of $Z$, hence ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z = \gamma_Z({\mathscr{O}}_Z)$ is an iterated extension of the sheaf ${\mathscr{E}}_z = \gamma_Z({\mathscr{O}}_z)$. Now the last part of Lemma~\ref{lemma:e-z-small} implies the last part of the proposition.

nodes.statement: Let $Z \cong \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m) \subset Z_d$ be a connected component. We apply Lemma~\ref{lemma:sheaves-y-z} to construct a sheaf ${\mathscr{E}}_Z$ on~$X \times Z$ such that ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z \cong p_{X*}{\mathscr{E}}_Z$. For this, first, note that the filtration on ${\mathscr{O}}_Z$ induced by the natural action of the ring ${\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m$ has quotients isomorphic to ${\mathscr{O}}_z$, where $z$ is the closed point of $Z$, hence the induced filtration on ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z \cong \gamma_Z({\mathscr{O}}_Z)$ has quotients isomorphic to $\gamma({\mathscr{O}}_z) = {\mathscr{E}}_z$, i.e., \begin{equation} (t^i{\mathfrak{E}}_Z)/(t^{i+1}{\mathfrak{E}}_Z) \cong {\mathscr{E}}_z. \end{equation} It is clear that the epimorphisms between these quotients induced by $t$ have to be isomorphisms, hence the sheaf ${\mathscr{E}}_Z$ associated with ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z$ is flat over~$Z$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma:sheaves-y-z}. Next, we define ${\mathscr{E}}_{Z_d}$ as the sum ${\mathscr{E}}_{Z_d} := \bigoplus {\mathscr{E}}_Z$ over connected components $Z \subset Z_d$. Then the first part of the proposition holds. It remains to show that the functors $\gamma_{Z_d}$ are Fourier--Mukai. The functor $\tilde\gamma_Z \colon {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_m) \to {\mathbf{D}}({\widetilde{X}})$ by construction (which is explained in Proposition~\ref{proposition:tcai-auslander} and is based on Proposition~\ref{proposition:rm-equivalence}) is a Fourier--Mukai functor. By~\eqref{def:gamma} the functor $\gamma_Z \colon {\mathbf{D}}(Z) \to {\mathbf{D}}(X)$ is also a Fourier--Mukai functor. Since the scheme $Z$ is affine, the kernel object defining the functor $\gamma_Z$ can be identified with the sheaf $\gamma_Z({\mathscr{O}}_Z) \cong {\mathfrak{E}}_Z \in {\mathbf{D}}(X)$ with its natural module structure over ${\mathsf{k}}[Z] = {\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m$, which corresponds to the sheaf ${\mathscr{E}}_Z$ by its definition above. The last claim follows from this by dualization (note that Grothendieck duality implies that the equivalence of Lemma~\ref{lemma:sheaves-y-z} is compatible with dualization, since the dualizing complex of $Z$ is trivial).

nodes.statement: By Corollary~\ref{corollary:pis-epi} we can write ${\mathscr{F}} = \pi_*{\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}$ for some ${\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}} \in {\mathbf{D}}({\widetilde{X}})$, hence by adjunction \begin{equation*} \chi({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_d}, {\mathscr{F}}) = \chi({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_d},\pi_*{\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}) = \chi(\pi^*{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_d},{\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}) = \chi({\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_{Z_d},{\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}). \end{equation*} As it is explained in Proposition~\ref{proposition:e-z-big} the bundle ${\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_{Z_2}$ is an extension (possibly trivial) of the line bundles~${\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_i)$ for $i = 1,2,3$, hence \begin{equation*} \mathrm{ch}({\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_{Z_2}) = \sum \mathrm{ch}({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_i)) = 3 + (3h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3) = 3 - K_{\widetilde{X}} = 2\mathrm{ch}({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}) + \mathrm{ch}(\omega_{\widetilde{X}}^{-1}) - 3\mathrm{ch}({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{P}}), \end{equation*} where ${\widetilde{P}}$ is a general point on ${\widetilde{X}}$. Therefore, by Riemann--Roch and adjunction we have \begin{equation*} \chi({\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_{Z_2},{\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}) = 2\chi({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}},{\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}) + \chi(\omega_{\widetilde{X}}^{-1},{\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}) - 3\chi({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{P}},{\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}) = 2\chi({\mathscr{O}}_X,{\mathscr{F}}) + \chi(\omega_X^{-1},{\mathscr{F}}) - 3\chi({\mathscr{O}}_{\pi({\widetilde{P}})},{\mathscr{F}}), \end{equation*} which gives the first equality. Similarly, for ${\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_{Z_3}$ we have \begin{equation*} \mathrm{ch}({\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_{Z_3}) = \mathrm{ch}({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h)) + \mathrm{ch}({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)) = \mathrm{ch}({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}) + \mathrm{ch}(\omega_{\widetilde{X}}^{-1}) - 2\mathrm{ch}({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{P}}), \end{equation*} and using Riemann--Roch and adjunction in the same way as before, we finish the proof.

nodes.statement: Let $Z \cong \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m)$ be a connected component of $Z_d$ with $d \in \{2,3\}$ with closed point~$z$. Consider the fiber square \begin{equation*} \xymatrix{ X \times Z \ar[r]^-{p_Z} \ar[d]_{p_X} & Z \ar[d] \\ X \ar[r] & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) } \end{equation*} The pushforward to $\mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}})$ of $p_{Z*}{\mathscr{E}}_{Z}$ equals the pushforward of $p_{X*}({\mathscr{E}}_{Z}) \cong {\mathfrak{E}}_Z$, i.e.~$H^\bullet(X,{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z})$ with its natural ${\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m$-module structure. So, by Lemma~\ref{lemma:sheaves-y-z} to check that $p_{Z*}{\mathscr{E}}_{Z}$ is a vector bundle it is enough to show that the natural epimorphisms between the quotient spaces $(t^iH^0(X,{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z}))/(t^{i+1}H^0(X,{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z}))$ are isomorphisms (the other cohomology groups of ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z$ vanish by Proposition~\ref{proposition:e-z-big}). By~\eqref{eq:fez-quotients} all these quotients are isomorphic to $H^0(X,{\mathscr{E}}_z)$, hence $d$-dimensional by Lemma~\ref{lemma:e-z-small}, hence the epimorphisms $t$ between them are isomorphisms. This proves that $p_{Z*}{\mathscr{E}}_{Z}$ is locally free of rank~$d$ on $Z$. For the second statement, let $Z \subset Z_2$ and $Z' \subset Z_3$ be connected components, $Z \cong \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m)$, and~$Z' \cong \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t']/(t')^{m'})$. Under an analogue of Lemma~\ref{lemma:sheaves-y-z} the sheaf $p_{23*}(p_{X2}^*{\mathscr{E}}_{Z_2}^\vee \otimes p_{X3}^*{\mathscr{E}}_{Z_3})$ corresponds to the vector space $H^\bullet(X,{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_2}^\vee \otimes {\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3})$ with its natural bifiltration. So, we have to check that the operators $t$ and $t'$ induce isomorphisms between the quotients of this bifiltration. Since \begin{equation*} H^\bullet(X,{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_2}^\vee \otimes {\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}) \cong \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_2},{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}) \cong \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet(\pi^*{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_2},\pi^*{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}) \cong \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_{Z_2},{\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_{Z_3}), \end{equation*} and the bifiltration is induced by the defining exact sequences~\eqref{eq:tcez-12}, \eqref{eq:tcez-12-23} and~\eqref{eq:tcez-123} of ${\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z$ and ${\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_{Z'}$, it is enough to compute $\mathrm{Ext}$-spaces between the corresponding line bundles on ${\widetilde{X}}$. A direct computation gives \begin{alignat*}{3} & \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_i),{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h)) &&\cong H^\bullet({\widetilde{X}},{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(e_i)) &&= {\mathsf{k}},\\ & \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_i),{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)) &&\cong H^\bullet({\widetilde{X}},{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_j - e_k)) &&= {\mathsf{k}}, \end{alignat*} therefore, the epimorphisms $t$ and $t'$ between them are isomorphisms, and the sheaf $p_{23*}(p_{X2}^*{\mathscr{E}}_{Z_2}^\vee \otimes p_{X3}^*{\mathscr{E}}_{Z_3})$ is locally free of rank 1 on $Z \times Z'$. Summing up over all connected components completes the proof of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Check isomorphisms of t-quotients of cohomology using Lemma sheaves-y-z and Ext computations on X~.

nodes.statement: As we already mentioned, $r({\mathscr{E}}_z) = 1$ implies the leading monomial of $h_{{\mathscr{E}}_z}$ equals $3t^2$. So, to show an equality of polynomials $h_{{\mathscr{E}}_z} = h_d$ it is enough to check that they take the same values at points~$t = 0$ and~$t = -1$. In other words, we have to check that \begin{equation*} \chi(X,{\mathscr{E}}_z) = h_d(0) = d \qquad\text{and}\qquad \chi(X,{\mathscr{E}}_z \otimes \omega_X) = h_d(-1) = 0. \end{equation*} The first is proved in Lemma~\ref{lemma:e-z-small}, and the second follows from ${\mathscr{E}}_z \in {\mathcal{A}}_d$ and decompositions~\eqref{eq:dbx-other}. The sheaf ${\mathscr{E}}_z$ is torsion free since by Lemma~\ref{lemma:e-z-small} it is the direct image of a line bundle under a dominant map $\pi$, hence is stable by Lemma~\ref{lemma:hd-stable}. Furthermore, it follows from Proposition~\ref{proposition:e-z-big} that ${\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_d}$ is semistable with the same reduced Hilbert polynomial. To show that ${\mathscr{E}}_z^\vee$ is a sheaf, consider the connected component $Z$ of~$Z_d$ containing~$z$ and note that the sheaf ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z$ is filtered by ${\mathscr{E}}_z$, hence ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z^\vee$ is filtered by ${\mathscr{E}}_z^\vee$. But ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z$ is locally free by Proposition~\ref{proposition:e-z-big}, hence~${\mathfrak{E}}_Z^\vee$ is a sheaf, hence ${\mathscr{E}}_z^\vee$ is a sheaf as well. Stability of ${\mathscr{E}}_z^\vee$ is proved in the same way as that of ${\mathscr{E}}_z$; and the fact that its Hilbert polynomial equals $h_d(-t-1)$ follows easily from Serre duality (Proposition~\ref{proposition:serre-gorenstein}).

nodes.statement: First, assume $d = 2$. Let us show that ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathcal{A}}_2$. By Corollary~\ref{corollary:a-as-orthogonals} for this we should check that~$\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{O}}_X) = \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3},{\mathscr{F}}) = 0$. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:hd-stable} the sheaf ${\mathscr{F}}$ is stable. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:hilbert-fz} and~\eqref{eq:hd-inequalities}, we have $\frac1{\ell(Z_3)}h_{{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}}(t) > h_{\mathscr{F}}(t) > h_{{\mathscr{O}}_X}(t)$, hence by semistability \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Hom}({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3},{\mathscr{F}}) = \mathrm{Hom}({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{O}}_X) = 0. \end{equation*} Similarly, $\frac1{\ell(Z_3)}h_{{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}}(t-1) < h_{\mathscr{F}}(t) < h_{{\mathscr{O}}_X}(t+1)$, hence \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Hom}({\mathscr{F}},{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}(K_X)) = \mathrm{Hom}({\mathscr{O}}_X(-K_X),{\mathscr{F}}) = 0. \end{equation*} By Serre duality on $X$ (note that ${\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}$ is locally free and use Proposition~\ref{proposition:serre-gorenstein}) we deduce \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Ext}^2({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3},{\mathscr{F}}) = \mathrm{Ext}^2({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{O}}_X) = 0. \end{equation*} Since (again by Serre duality and local freeness of ${\mathscr{O}}_X$ and ${\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}$) we can have nontrivial $\mathrm{Ext}^p({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3},{\mathscr{F}})$ and~$\mathrm{Ext}^p({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{O}}_X)$ only for $p \in \{0,1,2\}$, it remains to check that \begin{equation*} \chi({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3},{\mathscr{F}}) = \chi(X,{\mathscr{F}}(K_X)) = 0. \end{equation*} The second equality here just follows from $h_{\mathscr{F}}(-1) = h_2(-1) = 0$, and the first follows from Lemma~\ref{lemma:chi-ez-f} and $h_2(0) + h_2(-1) - 2 = 0$. Thus, we have shown that ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathcal{A}}_2 \cong {\mathbf{D}}(Z_2)$. Since $Z_2$ is a zero-dimensional scheme, any object in~${\mathbf{D}}(Z_2)$ is isomorphic to an iterated extension of shifts of structure sheaves of closed points in~$Z_2$. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:e-z-small} these sheaves correspond to sheaves~${\mathscr{E}}_z \in {\mathcal{A}}_2$, hence ${\mathscr{F}}$ is an extension of shifts of those. Since ${\mathscr{F}}$ is a pure sheaf of rank equal to~1, we conclude that ${\mathscr{F}} \cong {\mathscr{E}}_z$ for a closed point $z \in Z_2$. The case $d = 3$ is treated similarly. The same argument with~${\mathcal{A}}_2$ and~${\mathcal{A}}_3$ replaced by~${\mathcal{A}}_2^\vee \otimes \omega_X^{-1}$ and~${\mathcal{A}}_3^\vee \otimes \omega_X^{-1}$ and~\eqref{eq:dbx} replaced by a twist of~\eqref{eq:dbx-dual} proves part~$(ii)$.
nodes.statement_short: Show F lies in A_2 by orthogonality via stability, Serre duality and Euler characteristics, then use rank one.
