nodes.statement: For the first part note, that ${\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ is regular by Proposition~\ref{proposition:smoothness}, and in particular normal. Hence it is isomorphic to the normal closure of $S$ in the field of rational functions on ${\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}_0/S_0)$. The same argument works for ${\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)$, hence $\varphi_0$ extends to an isomorphism $\varphi$. The second claim is evident because the restriction morphisms $\mathrm{Br}({\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)) \to \mathrm{Br}({\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}_0/S_0))$ and~$\mathrm{Br}({\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)) \to \mathrm{Br}({\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'_0/S_0))$ of the Brauer groups are injective.
nodes.statement_short: Regular hence normal Z_d is the normalization of S in its function field; Brauer restriction injective.

nodes.statement: Assume $d \in \{2,3\}$. nodes.statement: Let ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ and ${\mathscr{X}}' \to S$ be two du Val families of sextic del Pezzo surfaces with regular total spaces ${\mathscr{X}}$ and ${\mathscr{X}}'$. Assume for $d \in \{2,3\}$ there is a birational $S$-isomorphism $\psi \colon \xymatrix@1{F_d({\mathscr{X}}/S) \ar@{-->}[r]^-{\sim} & F_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)}$. Then it induces a biregular isomorphism $\varphi \colon {\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } {\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)$ over~$S$ and we have $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)} = \varphi^*\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)}$.
nodes.name: Birational Hilbert schemes give isomorphic Z_d
nodes.statement_short: A birational S-isomorphism of F_d for regular families induces an isomorphism of Z_d preserving Brauer classes.

nodes.statement: Recall that ${\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ is the base of the maximal rationally connected fibration for the morphism~$F_d({\mathscr{X}}/S) \to S$. Therefore, the birational isomorphism $\psi$ of Hilbert schemes induces a birational isomorphism $\varphi_0$ over~$S$ of ${\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ and ${\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)$. Using Corollary~\ref{corollary:birational-isomorphism-zd} we deduce that it extends to an isomorphism $\varphi \colon {\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } {\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)$. Furthermore, since $F_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ is a Severi--Brauer variety associated with the Brauer class $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)}$ of order~$2$ or~$3$, the birational isomorphism of Hilbert schemes implies that either $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)} = \varphi^*\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)}$ or~$d = 3$ and~$\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)} = \varphi^*\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)}^{-1}$. In the latter case we replace~$\varphi$ by its composition with the involution $\sigma_{3,3}$ defined in Proposition~\ref{proposition:md-zd}.
nodes.statement_short: Z_d is the base of the MRC fibration of F_d; extend via Corollary birational-isomorphism-zd; fix the Brauer class with sigma_{3,3}.

nodes.statement: Let ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ be a generically smooth du Val family of sextic del Pezzo surfaces with regular total space~${\mathscr{X}}$. \noindent$(1)$ The Brauer class $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}$ vanishes if and only if the family ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ has a rational $3$-multisection. \noindent$(2)$ The Brauer class $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}$ vanishes if and only if the family ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ has a rational $2$-multisection.
nodes.name: Brauer classes and rational multisections
nodes.statement_short: beta_2 (resp. beta_3) vanishes iff the family has a rational 3- (resp. 2-) multisection.
assumptions: ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ be a generically smooth du Val family of sextic del Pezzo surfaces with regular total space~${\mathscr{X}}$
conclusions: The Brauer class $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}$ vanishes if and only if the family ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ has a rational $3$-multisection
The Brauer class $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}$ vanishes if and only if the family ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ has a rational $2$-multisection

nodes.statement: Note that the assumption implies that $S$, ${\mathscr{Z}}_2$, and ${\mathscr{Z}}_3$ are all regular (Proposition~\ref{proposition:smoothness}). Furthermore, by base change to an open subscheme in $S$ we may assume that ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ is smooth (hence ${\mathscr{Z}}_d \to S$ are smooth as well by Remark~\ref{remark:smoothness}). If $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}$ vanishes then the map $F_2({\mathscr{X}}) \to {\mathscr{Z}}_2$ has a rational section. Moreover, one can assume that such a rational section is not contained in the rational $2$-multisection of $F_2({\mathscr{X}}) \to {\mathscr{Z}}_2$ that parameterizes singular conics on fibers of ${\mathscr{X}}$. This means that there is a birational morphism ${\mathscr{Z}}'_2 \to {\mathscr{Z}}_2$ and a subscheme~${\mathscr{C}} \subset {\mathscr{X}} \times_S {\mathscr{Z}}'_2$ which is a family of conics on fibers of ${\mathscr{X}}$ with the general fiber over~${\mathscr{Z}}'_2$ a union of three smooth conics from distinct linear systems on a smooth sextic del Pezzo surface. Note that smooth conics from different linear systems intersect at a point, hence the projection ${\mathscr{C}} \to {\mathscr{X}}$ fails to be an isomorphism onto its image over a subscheme of ${\mathscr{X}}$ which is a rational 3-multisection of ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$. Similarly, if $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}$ vanishes then the map $F_3({\mathscr{X}}) \to {\mathscr{Z}}_3$ has a nice rational section, hence there is a birational morphism ${\mathscr{Z}}'_3 \to {\mathscr{Z}}_3$ and a subscheme~${\mathscr{C}} \subset {\mathscr{X}} \times_S {\mathscr{Z}}'_3$ which is a family of rational cubics on fibers of ${\mathscr{X}}$ with the general fiber over~${\mathscr{Z}}'_3$ a union of two smooth cubics from distinct linear systems on a smooth sextic del Pezzo surface. Smooth cubics from different linear systems intersect at two points, hence the projection ${\mathscr{C}} \to {\mathscr{X}}$ fails to be an isomorphism onto its image over a subscheme of ${\mathscr{X}}$ which is a rational 2-multisection of ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$. Conversely, assume a 2-multisection of ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ exists, i.e., there is a proper subscheme $T \subset {\mathscr{X}}$ such that the map $T \to S$ is generically finite of degree~2. In the Hilbert scheme $F_3({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ consider the subscheme $F_3^T({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ that parameterizes cubic curves containing the fibers of~$T$ over~$S$. Since on a smooth del Pezzo surface in each linear system of cubic curves there is either a unique curve containing a given pair of points (if the points do not lie on a line), or a pencil of such cubic curves (otherwise), we conclude that $F_3^T({\mathscr{X}}/S) \subset F_3({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ is either a rational section of $F_3({\mathscr{X}}/S) \to {\mathscr{Z}}_3$ or is generically a sub-${\mathbb{P}}^1$-bundle. In both cases it follows that the Brauer class $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}$ vanishes generically over~${\mathscr{Z}}_3$, and since~${\mathscr{Z}}_3$ is regular, $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3} = 0$. Similarly, if a 3-multisection $T$ of ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ exists, we consider the subscheme $F_4^T({\mathscr{X}}/S) \subset F_4({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ that parameterizes quartic curves containing the fibers of~$T$ over~$S$. Since on a smooth del Pezzo surface in each linear system of quartic curves there is either a unique curve containing a given triple of points (if the points do not lie on a conic), or a pencil of such curves (if the points lie on a conic, but not on a line), or a 2-dimensional linear system (otherwise), we conclude that $F_4^T({\mathscr{X}}/S) \subset F_4({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ is either a rational section of $F_4({\mathscr{X}}/S) \to {\mathscr{Z}}_4 = {\mathscr{Z}}_2$ (in the first case), or is generically a sub-${\mathbb{P}}^2$-bundle (in the third case), while in the second case the subscheme~$F_2^T({\mathscr{X}}/S) \subset F_2({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ provides a rational section of $F_2({\mathscr{X}}/S) \to {\mathscr{Z}}_2$. In all cases it follows that the Brauer class $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}$ vanishes generically over~${\mathscr{Z}}_2$, and since~${\mathscr{Z}}_2$ is regular, $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2} = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Rational sections of Severi-Brauer schemes give multisections via intersections of conics/cubics, and conversely.

nodes.statement: Assume the base field ${\mathsf{k}}$ is algebraically closed. The intersection $X_K$ defined by~\textup{\eqref{eq:xk}} is a sextic du Val del Pezzo surface if and only if \begin{itemize} \item the line ${\mathbb{P}}(K)$ does not intersect the dual Segre variety ${\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2^\vee) \subset {\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)$, and \item the line ${\mathbb{P}}(K)$ is not contained in the discriminant cubic hypersurface ${\mathscr{D}}_{W_1,W_2} \subset {\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)$. \end{itemize} Furthermore, $X_K$ is smooth if and only if the line ${\mathbb{P}}(K)$ is transversal to ${\mathscr{D}}_{W_1,W_2}$.

nodes.label: lemma:xk-duval

nodes.statement: First, let us show that the condition is necessary. If ${\mathbb{P}}(K)$ intersects ${\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2^\vee)$ then $K$ contains a bilinear form $b \in W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee$ of rank 1, i.e., $b = \varphi_1 \otimes \varphi_2$, where $\varphi_i \in W_i^\vee$. The zero locus of~$b$ on ${\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2)$ is equal to $({\mathbb{P}}(\varphi_1^\perp) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2)) \cup ({\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(\varphi_2^\perp))$. Consequently, $X_K$ is its hyperplane section, hence is a union of two cubic scrolls, hence is not an integral surface. Next, assume that ${\mathbb{P}}(K)$ is contained in ${\mathscr{D}}_{W_1,W_2}$. Then there are three possibilities: either \begin{itemize} \item $K \subset w_1^\perp \otimes W_2^\vee$ for some $w_1 \in W_1$, or \item $K \subset W_1^\vee \otimes w_2^\perp$ for some $w_2 \in W_2$, or \item $K \subset \mathrm{Ker}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee \to U_1^\vee \otimes U_2^\vee)$ for some 2-dimensional subspaces $U_1 \subset W_1$ and $U_2 \subset W_2$. \end{itemize} In the first case we have $\{w_1\} \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2) \subset X_K$, in the second case ${\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times \{w_2\} \subset X_K$, and in the third case ${\mathbb{P}}(U_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(U_2) \subset X_K$, so in all these cases the surface $X_K$ is not integral. Now, let us show that the conditions are sufficient. So, assume $K \subset W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee$ is such that the line~${\mathbb{P}}(K)$ is not contained in ${\mathscr{D}}_{W_1,W_2}$ and does not intersect ${\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2^\vee)$. Let $b_0 \in K$ be a bilinear form of rank 3 (it exists since ${\mathbb{P}}(K)$ is not contained in ${\mathscr{D}}_{W_1,W_2}$). Then $b_0$ identifies $W_2$ with $W_1^\vee$ and under this identification $b_0$ corresponds to the identity in ${\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_1) \cong {\mathbb{P}}(\mathrm{End}(W_1))$, so its zero locus is isomorphic to the flag variety $\mathrm{Fl}(1,2;W_1) \subset {\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee)$. The subspace $K$ is then determined by an operator $b \in \mathrm{End}(W_1)$ defined up to a scalar multiple of the identity, and the condition that ${\mathbb{P}}(K)$ does not intersect ${\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee) \otimes {\mathbb{P}}(W_2^\vee)$ can be rephrased by saying that the pencil $\{b + t\mathrm{id}\}$ does not contain operators of rank~1. From the Jordan Theorem it is clear that there are only three types of such $b$: \begin{itemize} \item[$(0)$] $b$ is diagonal with three distinct eigenvalues; \item[$(1)$] $b$ has two Jordan blocks of sizes 2 and 1 with distinct eigenvalues; \item[$(2)$] $b$ has one Jordan block of size 3. \end{itemize} It is easy to see that in case (0) the surface $X_b$ is smooth (hence of type 0), in case (1) it has one $A_1$ singularity (and is of type 2), and in case (3) it has one $A_2$ singularity (and is of type 4). It remains to note that case (0) happens precisely when the line ${\mathbb{P}}(K)$ is transversal to ${\mathscr{D}}_{W_1,W_2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Necessity: degenerate forms give reducible sections; sufficiency: normal forms of operators by Jordan theorem.

nodes.name: Reduce to an operator b up to scalars
nodes.statement: Let $b_0 \in K$ be a bilinear form of rank 3 (it exists since ${\mathbb{P}}(K)$ is not contained in ${\mathscr{D}}_{W_1,W_2}$). Then $b_0$ identifies $W_2$ with $W_1^\vee$ and under this identification $b_0$ corresponds to the identity in ${\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_1) \cong {\mathbb{P}}(\mathrm{End}(W_1))$, so its zero locus is isomorphic to the flag variety $\mathrm{Fl}(1,2;W_1) \subset {\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee)$. The subspace $K$ is then determined by an operator $b \in \mathrm{End}(W_1)$ defined up to a scalar multiple of the identity, and the condition that ${\mathbb{P}}(K)$ does not intersect ${\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee) \otimes {\mathbb{P}}(W_2^\vee)$ can be rephrased by saying that the pencil $\{b + t\mathrm{id}\}$ does not contain operators of rank~1. From the Jordan Theorem it is clear that there are only three types of such $b$:

nodes.label: proposition:dp-p2p2

nodes.statement: Using homological projective duality for ${\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2)$, see Theorem~\ref{theorem:hpd-p2p2}, we obtain from~\cite[Theorem~6.27]{kuznetsov2007hpd} a semiorthogonal decomposition \begin{equation*} {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}}) = \langle \Phi_{{\mathscr{E}}_2}({\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}) \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_2)), {\mathbf{D}}(S) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(1,0), {\mathbf{D}}(S) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(0,1), {\mathbf{D}}(S) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(1,1) \rangle, \end{equation*} where ${\mathbb{Y}}_2 \to {\mathscr{D}}_{W_1,W_2}$ is the resolution of singularities defined in~\eqref{eq:def-yy2}, and ${\mathscr{E}}_2$ is the derived pullback of the sheaf ${\mathbb{E}}_2$ defined by~\eqref{eq:hpd-kernel-xx3} with respect to the natural map \begin{equation} {\mathscr{X}} \times_S ({\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}) \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_2) \to {\mathscr{X}}_2 \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_2 \end{equation} (we will discuss this map below), where ${\mathscr{X}}_2$ is the universal hyperplane section of ${\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2)$. Mutating the last component to the far left (note that $K_{\mathscr{X}} = {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(-1,-1)$ in the relative Picard group~$\mathrm{Pic}({\mathscr{X}}/S)$), we get \begin{equation} {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}}) = \langle {\mathbf{D}}(S) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}, \Phi_{{\mathscr{E}}_2}({\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}) \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_2)), {\mathbf{D}}(S) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(1,0), {\mathbf{D}}(S) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(0,1) \rangle. \end{equation} We claim that this decomposition agrees with the general decomposition~\eqref{eq:dbcx-again} of a du Val family of sextic del Pezzo surfaces. Indeed, the last two components of~\eqref{eq:sod-cx-p2p2} can be considered as the derived category of~$S \sqcup S$ (the trivial double covering of $S$) embedded via the Fourier--Mukai functor with kernel \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{E}}_3 := {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(1,0) \sqcup {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(0,1) \in {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}} \sqcup {\mathscr{X}}) = {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}} \times_S (S \sqcup S)), \end{equation*} and the second component is the derived category of \begin{equation*} {\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}) \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_2 = {\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}) \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathscr{D}}_{W_1,W_2} \end{equation*} (recall that ${\mathbb{Y}}_2$ maps birationally onto ${\mathscr{D}}_{W_1,W_2}$ and ${\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}})$ by definition of $S$ does not touch the indeterminacy locus ${\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2^\vee)$ of that birational isomorphism), which is a flat degree~3 covering of~$S$ (since ${\mathscr{D}}_{W_1,W_2}$ is a hypersurface of degree~3), and it is embedded into~${\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}})$ via the Fourier--Mukai functor with kernel~${\mathscr{E}}_2$. Let us check that both ${\mathscr{E}}_2$ and ${\mathscr{E}}_3$ are flat families of torsion-free rank 1 sheaves on fibers of~${\mathscr{X}}$ over~$S$ with Hilbert polynomials $h_2(t)$ and $h_3(t)$ respectively, parameterized by the schemes \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{Z}}'_2 := {\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}) \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_2 \qquad\text{and}\qquad {\mathscr{Z}}'_3 := S \sqcup S. \end{equation*} For the second family flatness is clear and Hilbert polynomial computation is straightforward, so we skip it. For the first family we note that the map~\eqref{eq:map-cx2} is flat. Indeed, by~\eqref{eq:cx-p2p2} we have \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{X}} \times_S ({\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}) \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_2) = \Big(({\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2)) \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1 \otimes W_2)} {\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}^\perp)\Big) \times_S \Big({\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}) \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_2\Big), \end{equation*} while \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{X}}_2 \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_2 = ({\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2)) \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1 \otimes W_2)} Q \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_2, \end{equation*} where $Q \subset {\mathbb{P}}(W_1 \otimes W_2) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)$ is the incidence quadric, so the map~\eqref{eq:map-cx2} is induced by the natural map ${\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}^\perp) \times_S {\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}) \to Q = \mathrm{Fl}(1,8;W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)$. This map factors as \begin{equation*} {\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}^\perp) \times_S {\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}) \hookrightarrow {\mathbb{P}}_{\mathrm{Gr}(2,W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)}({\mathscr{K}}^\perp) \times_{\mathrm{Gr}(2,W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathbb{P}}_{\mathrm{Gr}(2,W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)}({\mathscr{K}}) = \mathrm{Fl}(1,2,8;W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee) \to Q. \end{equation*} The first map is an open embedding, while the last map is a ${\mathbb{P}}^6$-bundle, so the composition is flat (and even smooth). Recall the embedding of the Weil divisor ${\mathbb{Y}}_2 \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2) \hookrightarrow {\mathscr{X}}_2 \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_2$ defined by~\eqref{diagram:yy-cx3}. Its preimage under the map~\eqref{eq:map-cx2} is a Weil divisor in ${\mathscr{X}} \times_S ({\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}) \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_2)$ such that for any geometric point~$(K,b,w_1)$ of ${\mathscr{Z}}'_2 := {\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}) \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_2$ its fiber is the Weil divisor \begin{equation*} L := X_K \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)} \{w_1\} \subset X_K, \end{equation*} i.e., a line on the sextic del Pezzo surface $X_K$ contracted by the projection $X_K \to {\mathbb{P}}(W_1)$ to the point~$\{w_1\} \in {\mathbb{P}}(W_1)$. Thus, by~\eqref{eq:hpd-kernel-xx3}, the sheaf we are interested in is the twisted ideal ${\mathscr{I}}_L \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(1)$. In particular, it is torsion-free, and its Hilbert polynomial equals~$h_2(t)$. Therefore, the families of sheaves ${\mathscr{E}}_2$ and ${\mathscr{E}}_3$ induce maps \begin{equation*} \mu_2 \colon {\mathscr{Z}}'_2 \to {\mathscr{Z}}_2({\mathscr{X}}/S) \qquad\text{and}\qquad \mu_3 \colon {\mathscr{Z}}'_3 \to {\mathscr{Z}}_3({\mathscr{X}}/S) \end{equation*} such that the Brauer classes $\mu_2^*(\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2})$ and $\mu_3^*(\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3})$ are trivial and ${\mathscr{E}}_2$ and ${\mathscr{E}}_3$ are isomorphic (up to twists by line bundles on~${\mathscr{Z}}'_2$ and ${\mathscr{Z}}'_3$) to the pullbacks of the universal bundles ${\mathscr{E}}_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}$ and ${\mathscr{E}}_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}$, respectively. This means that for $d \in \{2,3\}$ we have isomorphisms of Fourier--Mukai functors \begin{equation*} \Phi_{{\mathscr{E}}_{d}} \cong \Phi_{{\mathscr{E}}_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d}} \circ \mu_{d*} \circ T_d \colon {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}'_d) \to {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}}), \end{equation*} where $T_d$ is a line bundle twist in ${\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}'_d)$. Since both $\Phi_{{\mathscr{E}}_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d}}$ and $\Phi_{{\mathscr{E}}_d}$ are fully faithful, so is the composition $\mu_{d*} \circ T_d \colon {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}'_d) \to {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}_d)$. Moreover, comparing semiorthogonal decompositions given by~\eqref{eq:dbcx-again} and~\eqref{eq:sod-cx-p2p2}, we conclude that $\mu_{d*} \circ T_d$ is essentially surjective, i.e., an equivalence of categories. Since $T_d$ is also an equivalence, we conclude that $\mu_{d*}$ is an equivalence, hence $\mu_d$ is an isomorphism. Thus ${\mathscr{Z}}'_d \cong {\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ and the Brauer classes $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}$ and $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}$ on~${\mathscr{Z}}_2({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ and~${\mathscr{Z}}_3({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ vanish.
nodes.statement_short: Apply HPD for P^2 x P^2 to get a decomposition, mutate, and identify its components with the universal families, forcing mu_d to be isomorphisms.

nodes.statement: Thus, by~\eqref{eq:hpd-kernel-xx3}, the sheaf we are interested in is the twisted ideal ${\mathscr{I}}_L \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(1)$. In particular, it is torsion-free, and its Hilbert polynomial equals~$h_2(t)$.
nodes.statement_short: Sheaves are twisted ideals of lines with polynomial h_2

nodes.name: Induced maps mu_d and isomorphism of functors
nodes.statement: Therefore, the families of sheaves ${\mathscr{E}}_2$ and ${\mathscr{E}}_3$ induce maps \begin{equation*} \mu_2 \colon {\mathscr{Z}}'_2 \to {\mathscr{Z}}_2({\mathscr{X}}/S) \qquad\text{and}\qquad \mu_3 \colon {\mathscr{Z}}'_3 \to {\mathscr{Z}}_3({\mathscr{X}}/S) \end{equation*} such that the Brauer classes $\mu_2^*(\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2})$ and $\mu_3^*(\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3})$ are trivial and ${\mathscr{E}}_2$ and ${\mathscr{E}}_3$ are isomorphic (up to twists by line bundles on~${\mathscr{Z}}'_2$ and ${\mathscr{Z}}'_3$) to the pullbacks of the universal bundles ${\mathscr{E}}_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}$ and ${\mathscr{E}}_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}$, respectively. This means that for $d \in \{2,3\}$ we have isomorphisms of Fourier--Mukai functors \begin{equation*} \Phi_{{\mathscr{E}}_{d}} \cong \Phi_{{\mathscr{E}}_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d}} \circ \mu_{d*} \circ T_d \colon {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}'_d) \to {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}}), \end{equation*} where $T_d$ is a line bundle twist in ${\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}'_d)$.
nodes.statement_short: Induced maps mu_d and isomorphism of functors

nodes.name: mu_d* is an equivalence
nodes.statement: Since both $\Phi_{{\mathscr{E}}_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d}}$ and $\Phi_{{\mathscr{E}}_d}$ are fully faithful, so is the composition $\mu_{d*} \circ T_d \colon {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}'_d) \to {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}_d)$. Moreover, comparing semiorthogonal decompositions given by~\eqref{eq:dbcx-again} and~\eqref{eq:sod-cx-p2p2}, we conclude that $\mu_{d*} \circ T_d$ is essentially surjective, i.e., an equivalence of categories. Since $T_d$ is also an equivalence, we conclude that $\mu_{d*}$ is an equivalence, hence $\mu_d$ is an isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: mu_d* is an equivalence

nodes.name: Z'_d = Z_d and trivial Brauer classes
nodes.statement: Thus ${\mathscr{Z}}'_d \cong {\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ and the Brauer classes $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}$ and $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}$ on~${\mathscr{Z}}_2({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ and~${\mathscr{Z}}_3({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ vanish.
nodes.statement_short: Z'_d = Z_d and trivial Brauer classes

nodes.statement: Considering the family $\bar{\mathscr{X}} \subset {\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2) \times \bar{S}$ of \emph{all} codimension 2 linear sections of~${\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2)$ over $\bar{S} := \mathrm{Gr}(2,W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)$ and applying the semiorthogonal decomposition of Theorem~\ref{theorem:hpd-p2p2}, we obtain \begin{equation*} {\mathbf{D}}(\bar{\mathscr{X}}) = \langle {\mathbf{D}}(\bar{S}), {\mathbf{D}}(\bar{{\mathscr{Z}}}_2), {\mathbf{D}}(\bar{{\mathscr{Z}}}_3) \rangle, \end{equation*} where $\bar{{\mathscr{Z}}_2} = {\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}) \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_2$ and $\bar{{\mathscr{Z}}_3} = \bar{S} \sqcup \bar{S}$. Note that the map $\bar{{\mathscr{Z}}_2} \to \bar{S}$ is not flat --- its non-flat locus $\bar{S} \setminus S$ is equal to the locus of non-integral fibers of the family $\bar{{\mathscr{X}}} \to \bar{S}$.

nodes.statement: Let ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ be a du Val family of sextic del Pezzo surfaces. If ${\mathscr{Z}}_3({\mathscr{X}}/S) = S \sqcup S$ and the Brauer class $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}$ is trivial, then Zariski locally over $S$ the family ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ can be represented as a family of codimension $2$ linear sections of\/ ${\mathbb{P}}^2 \times {\mathbb{P}}^2$. In particular, if ${\mathscr{X}}$ is regular then $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}$ is trivial.
nodes.name: Reconstructing a P^2 x P^2 family from Z_3
assumptions: If ${\mathscr{Z}}_3({\mathscr{X}}/S) = S \sqcup S$ and the Brauer class $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}$ is trivial
conclusions: In particular, if ${\mathscr{X}}$ is regular then $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}$ is trivial
nodes.label: lemma:reconstructing-family

nodes.statement: By Proposition~\ref{proposition:fd-md} there is a pair of rank 3 vector bundles ${\mathscr{W}}_1$ and ${\mathscr{W}}_2$ on $S$ such that \begin{equation*} F_3({\mathscr{X}}/S) = {\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{W}}_1) \sqcup {\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{W}}_2). \end{equation*} Moreover, the restrictions of the universal sheaf ${\mathscr{E}}_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}$ on ${\mathscr{X}} \times_S {\mathscr{Z}}_3 = {\mathscr{X}} \sqcup {\mathscr{X}}$ to the two components are line bundles defining regular maps ${\mathscr{X}} \to {\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{W}}_1)$ and ${\mathscr{X}} \to {\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{W}}_2)$ respectively. Thus, the induced map \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{X}} \to {\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{W}}_1) \times_S {\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{W}}_2) \end{equation*} is a closed embedding. Zariski locally the bundles ${\mathscr{W}}_1$ and ${\mathscr{W}}_2$ are trivial, hence we obtain the required local presentation of ${\mathscr{X}}$. The Brauer class $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}$ vanishes Zariski locally by Proposition~\ref{proposition:dp-p2p2} and~${\mathscr{Z}}_2$ is regular by Proposition~\ref{proposition:smoothness}, hence $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2} = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Projective bundles from F_3 = P(W_1) + P(W_2) give an embedding into P(W_1) x P(W_2).

nodes.statement: A slightly more general family of sextic del Pezzo surfaces can be obtained by replacing the projective spaces ${\mathbb{P}}(W_1)$ and ${\mathbb{P}}(W_2)$ by a pair of projectively dual (i.e., corresponding to mutually inverse Brauer classes) Severi--Brauer surfaces. In this way one can obtain a family of sextic del Pezzo surfaces with a nontrivial Brauer class $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}$ (however, this class will be ``constant in a family''). Another possible generalization, is to consider a double covering ${\tilde{S}} \to S$ and a Brauer class $\beta$ on ${\tilde{S}}$ of order~3 such that~$\beta = \sigma^*(\beta^{-1})$, where $\sigma \colon {\tilde{S}} \to {\tilde{S}}$ is the involution of the double covering (cf.~the isomorphism of Brauer classes in Proposition~\ref{proposition:md-zd}). Then one can apply the Weil restriction of scalars to obtain an \'etale locally trivial fibration over $S$ with fibers ${\mathbb{P}}^2 \times {\mathbb{P}}^2$, and then consider its linear section of codimension~2.
nodes.name: Generalizations via Severi-Brauer surfaces and Weil restriction
nodes.statement_short: Replacing P^2 x P^2 by dual Severi-Brauer surfaces or a Weil restriction gives families with nontrivial Brauer class beta_3.

Furthermore, $X_b$ is smooth if and only if $b \in {\mathbb{P}}(V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee) \setminus \overline{\mathrm{O}}_6$.

nodes.name: Base S of the (P^1)^3 family

nodes.statement: Let ${\mathscr{L}} \subset V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_S$ be the tautological line bundle, let ${\mathscr{L}}^\perp \subset V_1 \otimes V_2 \otimes V_3 \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_S$ be its rank 7 annihilator, and let \begin{equation} {\mathscr{X}} := ({\mathbb{P}}(V_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_2) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_3)) \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1 \otimes V_2 \otimes V_3)} {\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{L}}^\perp) \end{equation} be the corresponding du Val family of sextic del Pezzo surfaces.

nodes.name: Double cover D_{V1,V2,V3}

nodes.statement: Let ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ be the du Val family of sextic del Pezzo surfaces defined by~\textup{\eqref{eq:cx-p1p1p1}}. Then \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{Z}}_2 = S \sqcup S \sqcup S, \qquad {\mathscr{Z}}_3 = S \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee)} {{\mathscr{D}}_{V_1,V_2,V_3}}, \end{equation*} and the Brauer classes $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}$ and $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}$ are both trivial.

nodes.statement: The proof is parallel to that of Proposition~\ref{proposition:dp-p2p2}. Using homological projective duality for ${\mathbb{P}}(V_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_2) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_3)$, see Theorem~\ref{theorem:hpd-p1p1p1}, we obtain from~\cite[Theorem~6.27]{kuznetsov2007hpd} a semiorthogonal decomposition \begin{multline*} {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}}) = \langle \Phi_{{\mathscr{E}}_3}({\mathbf{D}}(S \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_3)), \\ {\mathbf{D}}(S) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(1,1,1), {\mathbf{D}}(S) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(2,1,1), {\mathbf{D}}(S) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(1,2,1), {\mathbf{D}}(S) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(1,1,2) \rangle, \end{multline*} where ${\mathbb{Y}}_3 \to {\mathscr{D}}_{V_1,V_2,V_3}$ is the resolution of singularities defined in~\eqref{eq:def-yy3} and where ${\mathscr{E}}_3$ is the derived pullback of the sheaf ${\mathbb{E}}_3$ defined by~\eqref{eq:hpd-kernel-xxx3} with respect to the natural map \begin{equation} {\mathscr{X}} \times_S (S \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_3) \to {\mathscr{X}}_3 \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_3 \end{equation} (we will discuss this map below). Mutating the last four components to the far left (again, note that~\mbox{$K_{\mathscr{X}} = {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(-1,-1,-1)$} in the relative Picard group~$\mathrm{Pic}({\mathscr{X}}/S)$), we get \begin{multline} {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}}) = \langle {\mathbf{D}}(S) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}, {\mathbf{D}}(S) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(1,0,0), {\mathbf{D}}(S) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(0,1,0), {\mathbf{D}}(S) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(0,0,1), \\ \Phi_{{\mathscr{E}}_3}({\mathbf{D}}(S \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_3)) \rangle. \end{multline} We claim that this decomposition agrees with the general decomposition~\eqref{eq:dbcx-again} for a du Val family of sextic del Pezzo surfaces. Indeed, its second, third and fourth components can be considered as the derived category of $S \sqcup S \sqcup S$ (the trivial triple covering of $S$) embedded via the Fourier--Mukai functor with kernel \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{E}}_2 := {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(1,0,0) \sqcup {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(0,1,0) \sqcup {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(0,0,1) \in {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}} \sqcup {\mathscr{X}} \sqcup {\mathscr{X}}) = {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}} \times_S (S \sqcup S \sqcup S)), \end{equation*} while the last component is the derived category of~$S \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_3 = S \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee)} {{\mathscr{D}}_{V_1,V_2,V_3}}$ (recall that ${\mathbb{Y}}_3$ maps birationally onto ${{\mathscr{D}}_{V_1,V_2,V_3}}$ and $S$ by definition does not touch the image $\overline{\mathrm{O}}_4$ (see Remark~\ref{remark:fibers-resolution-dvvv}) of the indeterminacy locus of that birational isomorphism), which is a flat degree~2 covering of~$S$ (since ${{\mathscr{D}}_{V_1,V_2,V_3}}$ is flat over the complement of~$\overline{\mathrm{O}}_4$), and it is embedded into~${\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}})$ via the Fourier--Mukai functor with kernel~${\mathscr{E}}_3$. Let us check that both ${\mathscr{E}}_2$ and ${\mathscr{E}}_3$ are flat families of torsion-free rank 1 sheaves on the fibers of ${\mathscr{X}}$ over~$S$ with Hilbert polynomials $h_2(t)$ and $h_3(t)$ respectively, parameterized by \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{Z}}'_2 := S \sqcup S \sqcup S \qquad\text{and}\qquad {\mathscr{Z}}'_3 := S \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_3. \end{equation*} For the first flatness is clear and Hilbert polynomial computation is straightforward, so we skip it. For the second we note that the map~\eqref{eq:map-cx3} is flat. Indeed, arguing as in the proof of Proposition~\ref{proposition:dp-p2p2} we can check that the map~\eqref{eq:map-cx3} is obtained by base change from the map \begin{equation*} {\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{L}}^\perp) \times_S {\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{L}}) \to Q = \mathrm{Fl}(1,7;V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee) \end{equation*} which is an open embedding. Recall the embedding of the Weil divisor ${\mathbb{Y}}_3 \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_3) \hookrightarrow {\mathscr{X}}_3 \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_3$ defined by~\eqref{diagram:yy-cx}. The preimage of ${\mathbb{Y}}_3 \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_3)$ under~\eqref{eq:map-cx3} is a Weil divisor in ${\mathscr{X}} \times_S (S \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_3)$ such that for any closed point $(b,v_1,v_2)$ of ${\mathscr{Z}}'_3 = S \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_3$ its fiber is the Weil divisor \begin{equation*} L := X_b \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_2)} \{(v_1,v_2)\} \subset X_b, \end{equation*} i.e., a line on the sextic del Pezzo surface $X_b$ contracted by the projection $X_b \to {\mathbb{P}}(V_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_2)$ to the point $(v_1,v_2) \in {\mathbb{P}}(V_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_2)$. Thus, by~\eqref{eq:hpd-kernel-xxx3}, the sheaf we are interested in is the twisted ideal \mbox{${\mathscr{I}}_L \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_2)}(1,1)$}. In particular, it is torsion-free, and its Hilbert polynomial equals~$h_3(t)$. The rest of the proof repeats the argument of Proposition~\ref{proposition:dp-p2p2}.

Identify components
nodes.statement: We claim that this decomposition agrees with the general decomposition~\eqref{eq:dbcx-again} for a du Val family of sextic del Pezzo surfaces. Indeed, its second, third and fourth components can be considered as the derived category of $S \sqcup S \sqcup S$ (the trivial triple covering of $S$) embedded via the Fourier--Mukai functor with kernel \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{E}}_2 := {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(1,0,0) \sqcup {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(0,1,0) \sqcup {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(0,0,1) \in {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}} \sqcup {\mathscr{X}} \sqcup {\mathscr{X}}) = {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}} \times_S (S \sqcup S \sqcup S)), \end{equation*} while the last component is the derived category of~$S \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_3 = S \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee)} {{\mathscr{D}}_{V_1,V_2,V_3}}$ (recall that ${\mathbb{Y}}_3$ maps birationally onto ${{\mathscr{D}}_{V_1,V_2,V_3}}$ and $S$ by definition does not touch the image $\overline{\mathrm{O}}_4$ (see Remark~\ref{remark:fibers-resolution-dvvv}) of the indeterminacy locus of that birational isomorphism), which is a flat degree~2 covering of~$S$ (since ${{\mathscr{D}}_{V_1,V_2,V_3}}$ is flat over the complement of~$\overline{\mathrm{O}}_4$), and it is embedded into~${\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}})$ via the Fourier--Mukai functor with kernel~${\mathscr{E}}_3$.
nodes.statement_short: Identify components

nodes.name: Kernels are flat families
nodes.statement: Let us check that both ${\mathscr{E}}_2$ and ${\mathscr{E}}_3$ are flat families of torsion-free rank 1 sheaves on the fibers of ${\mathscr{X}}$ over~$S$ with Hilbert polynomials $h_2(t)$ and $h_3(t)$ respectively, parameterized by \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{Z}}'_2 := S \sqcup S \sqcup S \qquad\text{and}\qquad {\mathscr{Z}}'_3 := S \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_3. \end{equation*} For the first flatness is clear and Hilbert polynomial computation is straightforward, so we skip it. For the second we note that the map~\eqref{eq:map-cx3} is flat. Indeed, arguing as in the proof of Proposition~\ref{proposition:dp-p2p2} we can check that the map~\eqref{eq:map-cx3} is obtained by base change from the map \begin{equation*} {\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{L}}^\perp) \times_S {\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{L}}) \to Q = \mathrm{Fl}(1,7;V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee) \end{equation*} which is an open embedding. Recall the embedding of the Weil divisor ${\mathbb{Y}}_3 \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_3) \hookrightarrow {\mathscr{X}}_3 \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_3$ defined by~\eqref{diagram:yy-cx}. The preimage of ${\mathbb{Y}}_3 \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_3)$ under~\eqref{eq:map-cx3} is a Weil divisor in ${\mathscr{X}} \times_S (S \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_3)$ such that for any closed point $(b,v_1,v_2)$ of ${\mathscr{Z}}'_3 = S \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_3$ its fiber is the Weil divisor \begin{equation*} L := X_b \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_2)} \{(v_1,v_2)\} \subset X_b, \end{equation*} i.e., a line on the sextic del Pezzo surface $X_b$ contracted by the projection $X_b \to {\mathbb{P}}(V_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_2)$ to the point $(v_1,v_2) \in {\mathbb{P}}(V_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_2)$. Thus, by~\eqref{eq:hpd-kernel-xxx3}, the sheaf we are interested in is the twisted ideal \mbox{${\mathscr{I}}_L \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_2)}(1,1)$}. In particular, it is torsion-free, and its Hilbert polynomial equals~$h_3(t)$.
nodes.statement_short: Kernels are flat families

The preimage of ${\mathbb{Y}}_3 \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_3)$ under~\eqref{eq:map-cx3} is a Weil divisor in ${\mathscr{X}} \times_S (S \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_3)$ such that for any closed point $(b,v_1,v_2)$ of ${\mathscr{Z}}'_3 = S \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1^\vee \otimes V_2^\vee \otimes V_3^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_3$ its fiber is the Weil divisor \begin{equation*} L := X_b \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_2)} \{(v_1,v_2)\} \subset X_b, \end{equation*} i.e., a line on the sextic del Pezzo surface $X_b$ contracted by the projection $X_b \to {\mathbb{P}}(V_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_2)$ to the point $(v_1,v_2) \in {\mathbb{P}}(V_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_2)$.

If ${\mathscr{Z}}_2({\mathscr{X}}/S) = S \sqcup S \sqcup S$ and the Brauer class $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}$ is trivial, then Zariski locally over $S$ the family ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ can be represented as a family of hyperplane sections of\/ ${\mathbb{P}}^1 \times {\mathbb{P}}^1 \times {\mathbb{P}}^1$. In particular, the anticanonical class of $\widehat{X}$ is nef and big and the anticanonical model of $\widehat{X}$ (i.e., the image of $\widehat{X}$ under the anticanonical map) is a sextic du Val del Pezzo surface.

Then \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{Z}}_2 \cong {\mathscr{Y}} \qquad\text{and}\qquad {\mathscr{Z}}_3 \cong S \,\mathop\cup\limits_{S_1}\, S, \end{equation*} and both Brauer classes $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}$ and $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}$ are trivial.

Let $S_{1,0} \subset S$ and $S_{0,1} \subset S$ be the divisors parameterizing subschemes contained in a horizontal or a vertical ruling of ${\mathbb{P}}^1 \times {\mathbb{P}}^1$ respectively. Then \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{Z}}_2 \cong S \,\mathop\cup\limits_{S_{1,0}}\, S \,\mathop\cup\limits_{S_{0,1}}\, S \qquad\text{and}\qquad {\mathscr{Z}}_3 \cong {\mathscr{Y}} \end{equation*} and both Brauer classes $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}$ and $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}$ are trivial.

nodes.statement: The algebra ${\tilde{R}}_m$ is defined as the path algebra of a quiver with relations: \begin{equation} {\tilde{R}}_m = {\mathsf{k}}\left\{\left. \xymatrix@1{\bullet \ar@<-.5ex>[r]_-{\beta_1} & \bullet \ar@<-.5ex>[l]_-{\alpha_1} \ar@<-.5ex>[r]_-{\beta_2} & \bullet \ar@<-.5ex>[l]_-{\alpha_2} \ar@{}[r]|-{\dots} & \bullet \ar@<-.5ex>[r]_-{\beta_{m-1}} & \bullet \ar@<-.5ex>[l]_-{\alpha_{m-1}} } \ \right|\ \text{$\beta_i\alpha_i = \alpha_{i+1}\beta_{i+1}$ for $1 \le i \le m-2$, $\beta_{m-1}\alpha_{m-1} = 0$}\ \right\}. \end{equation}
nodes.name: Auslander algebra R~_m
nodes.statement_short: R~_m is the path algebra of the A_m double quiver with relations beta_i alpha_i = alpha_{i+1} beta_{i+1}, beta_{m-1} alpha_{m-1} = 0.

nodes.statement: {\tilde{R}}_m = {\mathsf{k}}\left\{\left. \xymatrix@1{\bullet \ar@<-.5ex>[r]_-{\beta_1} & \bullet \ar@<-.5ex>[l]_-{\alpha_1} \ar@<-.5ex>[r]_-{\beta_2} & \bullet \ar@<-.5ex>[l]_-{\alpha_2} \ar@{}[r]|-{\dots} & \bullet \ar@<-.5ex>[r]_-{\beta_{m-1}} & \bullet \ar@<-.5ex>[l]_-{\alpha_{m-1}} } \ \right|\ \text{$\beta_i\alpha_i = \alpha_{i+1}\beta_{i+1}$ for $1 \le i \le m-2$, $\beta_{m-1}\alpha_{m-1} = 0$}\ \right\}.

nodes.statement: Using~\eqref{eq:projective-resolution-ei} we see that $\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet(E_i,E_j)$ is computed by the complex \begin{equation*} (E_j)_i \xrightarrow{\ \beta_{i+1}\ } (E_j)_{i+1}. \end{equation*} If $i > j$ both spaces are zero and if $i = j$ the first is ${\mathsf{k}}$ and the second is zero, hence the collection is exceptional. Similarly, if $j > i$ both spaces are ${\mathsf{k}}$ and the arrow is zero, hence $\mathrm{Hom}(E_i,E_j) = \mathrm{Ext}^1(E_i,E_j) = {\mathsf{k}}$. For the second statement, note that we have an exact sequence \begin{equation} 0 \to E_{i-1} \xrightarrow{\ \alpha_i\ } E_i \to S_i \to 0, \end{equation} which shows that for $j \le k$ the natural map $E_j \to E_k$ is injective and its cokernel is an extension of simple modules $S_l$ with $j+1 \le l \le k$. On the other hand, \eqref{eq:projective-resolution-ei} implies that $\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet(E_i,S_l) = 0$ as soon as~$l \ge i+2$, hence the map \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet(E_i,E_j) \to \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet(E_i,E_k) \end{equation*} induced by the embedding $E_j \to E_k$ is an isomorphism. This proves the case when $q = 0$. Similarly, merging~\eqref{eq:resolution-simple} with~\eqref{eq:projective-resolution-ei} we obtain for $l \ge 1$ a projective resolution \begin{equation} 0 \to P_l \xrightarrow{\ (-\alpha_{l+1},\beta_l)\ } P_{l+1} \oplus P_{l-1} \xrightarrow{\ (\beta_{l+1},\alpha_l)\ } P_l \to S_l \to 0 \end{equation} of the simple module $S_l$. It follows that $\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet(S_l,E_k)$ for $1 \le l < k$ are computed by the complex \begin{equation*} (E_k)_l \xrightarrow{\ (0,1)\ } (E_k)_{l+1} \oplus (E_k)_{l-1} \xrightarrow{\ (-1,0)} (E_k)_l, \end{equation*} hence for $1 \le l < k$ we have $\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet(S_l,E_k) = 0$. On the other hand, the cokernel of the embedding $E_i \to E_j$ is an extension of simple modules $S_l$ with $1 \le l \le j$, hence the map \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet(E_j,E_k) \to \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet(E_i,E_k) \end{equation*} induced by this embedding is an isomorphism. This proves the case when $p = 0$.

nodes.statement: Since the category ${\mathscr{T}}$ is enhanced, there is an equivalence of ${\mathscr{T}}$ with the derived category of the DG algebra $\mathrm{RHom}_{\mathscr{T}}(\oplus {\mathscr{L}}_i,\oplus {\mathscr{L}}_i)$. By the assumption, its cohomology is isomorphic (as a graded algebra) to the graded algebra $\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet_{{\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_m)}(\oplus E_i, \oplus E_i)$. To get the desired equivalence, it remains to check that the latter algebra (considered as a DG algebra with trivial differential) is formal. But formality is clear, since any higher $A_\infty$-operation ${\mathbf{m}}_i$ (with $i \ge 3$) requires at least three non-trivial arguments, so one needs the quiver to have at least four vertices to admit such an operation. So, for ${\tilde{R}}_2$ and ${\tilde{R}}_3$ all higher operations vanish and the algebra is formal.

nodes.statement: The functor $\pi_m^* \colon {\mathbf{D}}^-({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m) \to {\mathbf{D}}^-({\tilde{R}}_m)$ is fully faithful, and its right adjoint functor~$\pi_{m*} \colon {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_m) \to {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m)$ preserves boundedness and is essentially surjective. We have \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Ker} \pi_{m*} = \langle S_1,\dots,S_{m-1} \rangle^\oplus \qquad\text{and}\qquad \mathrm{Im} \pi_m^* = \langle P_0 \rangle^\oplus = {}^\perp\langle S_1,\dots,S_{m-1} \rangle. \end{equation*} Moreover, $\pi_{m*}(S_0) = {\mathsf{k}}$ and $\pi_{m*}(P_0) = {\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m$.

nodes.statement: The functor $\pi_m^*$ is fully faithful by~\cite[Theorem~5.23]{kuznetsov2015categorical} and $\pi_{m*} \circ \pi_m^* \cong \mathrm{id}$ by~\cite[(48)]{kuznetsov2015categorical}. Furthermore, $\pi_{m*}$ is exact by definition, hence for any $N \in {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m)$, taking $M := \tau^{\ge p}\pi_m^*(N)$ (the canonical truncation) with $p \ll 0$, we obtain $N \cong \pi_{m_*}M$, hence $\pi_{m*}$ is essentially surjective. The image of~$\pi_m^*$ by definition equals the subcategory $\langle P_0 \rangle^\oplus \subset {\mathbf{D}}^-({\tilde{R}}_m)$ and this category is evidently equal to the orthogonal of the simple modules $S_1$, \dots, $S_{m-1}$. Since the functor $\pi_{m*}$ is the right adjoint of~$\pi_m^*$, we have $\mathrm{Ker} \pi_{m*} = (\mathrm{Im} \pi_m^*)^\perp = P_0^\perp = \langle S_1,\dots,S_{m-1} \rangle^\oplus$. Finally, applying~\eqref{eq:pms} we easily get~$\pi_{m*}(S_0) = \epsilon_0S_0 = {\mathsf{k}}$ and $\pi_{m*}(P_0) = \epsilon_0P_0 = \epsilon_0{\tilde{R}}_m\epsilon_0 = ({\tilde{R}}_m)_{00} = {\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m$.

nodes.statement: The moduli stack ${\mathfrak{DP}_6}$ of sextic du Val del Pezzo surfaces is the fibered category over $(\mathrm{Sch}/{\mathsf{k}})$ whose fiber over a ${\mathsf{k}}$-scheme $S$ is the groupoid of all du Val $S$-families of sextic del Pezzo surfaces $f \colon {\mathscr{X}} \to S$ (in the sense of Definition~\ref{definition:family-dp6}). A morphism from $f' \colon {\mathscr{X}}' \to S'$ to $f \colon {\mathscr{X}} \to S$ is a fiber product diagram \begin{equation*} \xymatrix{ {\mathscr{X}}' \ar[r] \ar[d]_{f'} & {\mathscr{X}} \ar[d]^f \\ S' \ar[r] & S } \end{equation*}
nodes.section: B Moduli stack of sextic du Val del Pezzo surfaces
nodes.name: Moduli stack DP_6
nodes.statement_short: DP_6 is the fibered category of du Val families of sextic del Pezzo surfaces with fiber-product diagrams as morphisms.

nodes.statement: The moduli stack ${\mathfrak{DP}_6}$ is a smooth Artin stack of finite type over ${\mathsf{k}}$.

conclusions: The moduli stack ${\mathfrak{DP}_6}$ is a smooth Artin stack of finite type over ${\mathsf{k}}$

nodes.statement: By Hilbert scheme argument, the stack ${\mathfrak{DP}_6}$ is an Artin stack of finite type. So, by deformation theory it is enough to check that deformations of a sextic du Val del Pezzo surface $X$ over an algebraically closed field are unobstructed, i.e., that $\mathrm{Ext}^p(\Omega_X,{\mathscr{O}}_X) = 0$ for $p \ge 2$. On the other hand, since $X$ has isolated hypersurface singularities, the sheaf $\Omega_X$ has a locally free resolution of length~1, hence~$\mathscr{E}\mathit{xt}^p(\Omega_X,{\mathscr{O}}_X) = 0$ for $p \ge 2$ and $\mathscr{E}\mathit{xt}^1(\Omega_X,{\mathscr{O}}_X)$ has zero-dimensional support. By the local-to-global spectral sequence this means that \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Ext}^{\ge 2}(\Omega_X,{\mathscr{O}}_X) = H^{\ge 2}(X,T_X). \end{equation*} Since $X$ is a surface, we just have to check that $H^2(X,T_X) = 0$. This holds by~\cite[Proposition~3.1]{hacking2010smoothable}.

nodes.statement_short: Unobstructedness: Ext^2(Omega_X,O_X) = H^2(T_X) = 0 by Hacking-Prokhorov.

nodes.statement: The stack ${\mathfrak{DP}_6}$ is not separated --- one can construct two du Val families ${\mathscr{X}} \to {\mathbb{A}}^1$ and~${\mathscr{X}}' \to {\mathbb{A}}^1$ that are isomorphic over ${\mathbb{A}}^1 \setminus \{0\}$, but differ by a small birational transformation over the whole base. The simplest example is to consider the blowup ${\widehat{{\mathscr{X}}}} = \mathrm{Bl}_{{\mathscr{Y}}}({\mathbb{P}}^2 \times {\mathbb{A}}^1) \to {\mathbb{A}}^1$, where ${\mathscr{Y}} = \Big(\{(1,0,0)\} \times {\mathbb{A}}^1\Big) \sqcup \Big(\{(0,1,0)\} \times {\mathbb{A}}^1\Big) \sqcup \Big\{ ((1,1,t),t) \mid t \in {\mathbb{A}}^1 \Big\}$, and define ${\mathscr{X}} \to {\mathbb{A}}^1$ as the family of relative anticanonical models of ${\widehat{{\mathscr{X}}}}$. Then ${\mathscr{X}} \to {\mathbb{A}}^1$ is smooth over~${\mathbb{A}}^1 \times \{0\}$ and degenerates to a singular del Pezzo surface (of type 1) at point $t = 0$. On the other hand, the family ${\mathscr{X}} \times_{{\mathbb{A}}^1} ({\mathbb{A}}^1 \setminus \{0\}) \to {\mathbb{A}}^1 \setminus \{0\}$ is isomorphic to the trivial family, hence can be extended to a trivial family ${\mathscr{X}}' \to {\mathbb{A}}^1$. Thus, the families~${\mathscr{X}}$ and ${\mathscr{X}}'$ are isomorphic over ${\mathbb{A}}^1 \setminus \{0\}$, but have different fibers over $0$.

nodes.name: Non-separatedness of the moduli stack
nodes.statement_short: Two families over A^1, isomorphic off 0, with different fibers over 0, show DP_6 is not separated.

For this we mutate ${\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(2,0)$ and ${\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(0,2)$ to the far left. An easy computation shows that the result is the following exceptional collection \begin{equation*} {\mathbf{D}}({{\mathbb{X}}_2}) = \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(0,-1), {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(-1,0), {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}, {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(1,0), {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(0,1), {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(1,1), {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(2,1), {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(1,2), {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(2,2) \rangle. \end{equation*} Clearly, this is a rectangular Lefschetz collection with respect to ${\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(1,1)$ with three blocks equal to \begin{equation} {\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}^{\rm{sym}} = \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(0,-1), {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(-1,0), {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2} \rangle. \end{equation} It is symmetric with respect to the transposition of factors.

nodes.statement: The homological projective duality of ${\mathbb{X}}_2$ with respect to the standard Lefschetz decomposition \begin{equation*} {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{X}}_2) = \langle {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}(W_1)), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}(W_1)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(1,1), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}(W_1)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(2,2) \rangle \end{equation*} is described in~\cite{bernardara2016determinantal}. For this the linear homological projective duality argument~\cite[Section~8]{kuznetsov2007hpd} is used. Indeed, the scheme~${{\mathbb{X}}_2}$ can be considered as a projectivization of a vector bundle \begin{equation*} {{\mathbb{X}}_2} \cong {\mathbb{P}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}({\mathscr{W}}_2), \qquad {\mathscr{W}}_2 := W_2\otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(-1) \subset {\mathbb{W}} \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}. \end{equation*} Consequently, by~\cite[Corollary~8.3]{kuznetsov2007hpd} the homological projectively dual of ${{\mathbb{X}}_2}$ with respect to the Lefschetz decomposition with the first block ${\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}(W_1))$ is \begin{equation} {{\mathbb{Y}}_2} := {\mathbb{P}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}({\mathscr{W}}_2^\perp), \end{equation} where ${\mathscr{W}}_2^\perp := \mathrm{Ker}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)} \to {\mathscr{W}}_2^\vee) \cong W_2^\vee \otimes \Omega_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(1)$ is a rank 6 vector bundle on~${\mathbb{P}}(W_1)$.

nodes.statement: Let ${{\mathscr{X}}_2} \subset {{\mathbb{X}}_2} \times {\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)$ be the universal hyperplane section of ${{\mathbb{X}}_2}$. By~\cite[Theorem~8.2]{kuznetsov2007hpd}, there is a semiorthogonal decomposition \begin{equation} {\mathbf{D}}({{\mathscr{X}}_2}) = \langle i_*\phi^*({\mathbf{D}}({{\mathbb{Y}}_2})), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(1,1), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(2,2) \rangle, \end{equation} where the morphisms $i$ and $\phi$ are defined by the Cartesian diagram \begin{equation} \vcenter{\xymatrix{ {{\mathbb{Y}}_2} \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2) \ar[r]^-i \ar[d]_\phi & {{\mathscr{X}}_2} \ar[d]^{p_{{\mathscr{X}}_2}} \\ {{\mathbb{Y}}_2} \ar[r]^-{p_{{\mathbb{Y}}_2}} & {\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee) \ar[r]^-{p_2} & {\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee) }} \end{equation} and the map $p_{{\mathbb{Y}}_2}$ is induced by the embedding ${\mathscr{W}}_2^\perp \hookrightarrow {\mathbb{W}}^\vee \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}$. We modify~\eqref{eq:dbxx3-1} by a sequence of mutations to change it to the form we need. First, using the standard exceptional collection ${\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}(W_1)) = \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(-1), {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}, {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(1) \rangle$, decomposition \eqref{eq:dbxx3-1} can be rewritten as \begin{multline*} {\mathbf{D}}({{\mathscr{X}}_2}) = \langle i_*\phi^*({\mathbf{D}}({{\mathbb{Y}}_2})), \\ {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(0,1), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(1,1), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(2,1), \\ {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(1,2), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(2,2), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(3,2) \rangle. \end{multline*} Mutating the last component to the far left and taking into account that $\omega_{{\mathscr{X}}_2} \cong {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(-2,-2)$ up to a line bundle pulled back from ${\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)$, we obtain a semiorthogonal decomposition \begin{multline*} {\mathbf{D}}({{\mathscr{X}}_2}) = \langle {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(1,0), i_*\phi^*({\mathbf{D}}({{\mathbb{Y}}_2})), \\ {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(0,1), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(1,1), \\ {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(2,1), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(1,2), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(2,2) \rangle. \end{multline*} Next, mutating the second component one step to the left, we get \begin{multline} {\mathbf{D}}({{\mathscr{X}}_2}) = \langle \Phi({\mathbf{D}}({{\mathbb{Y}}_2})), \\ {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(1,0), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(0,1), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(1,1), \\ {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(2,1), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(1,2), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(2,2) \rangle. \end{multline} where $\Phi = {\mathbb{L}}_{{\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(1,0)} \circ i_* \circ \phi^* \colon {\mathbf{D}}({{\mathbb{Y}}_2}) \to {\mathbf{D}}({{\mathscr{X}}_2})$. This almost proves the result. The only small thing left is to show that the functor $\Phi$ is a Fourier--Mukai functor whose kernel is supported on the fiber product ${{\mathbb{Y}}_2} \times_{{\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)} {{\mathscr{X}}_2}$. For this we note that by~\eqref{diagram:yy-cx3} the functor $i_* \circ \phi^*$ is a Fourier--Mukai functor with kernel $j_*{\mathscr{O}}_{{{\mathbb{Y}}_2} \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2)}$, where $j \colon {\mathbb{Y}}_2 \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2) \to {\mathbb{Y}}_2 \times_{{\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)} {\mathscr{X}}_2$ is the embedding induced by the commutative square~\eqref{diagram:yy-cx3}. Moreover, using notation from the diagram~\eqref{diagram:yy-cx3}, the projection functor onto ${\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(1,0)$ is given by \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{F}} \mapsto p_{{\mathscr{X}}_2}^*(p_2^*p_{2*}(p_{{\mathscr{X}}_2*}{\mathscr{F}} \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(-1)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(1)), \end{equation*} and its composition with $i_* \circ \phi^*$ is given by \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{F}} \mapsto p_{{\mathscr{X}}_2}^*(p_2^*p_{2*}(p_{{\mathbb{Y}}_2*}{\mathscr{F}} \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(-1)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(1)). \end{equation*} In other words, this composition is a Fourier--Mukai functor with kernel $p_{{\mathbb{Y}}_2}^*({\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(-1)) \boxtimes p_{{\mathscr{X}}_2}^*({\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(1))$ on ${\mathbb{Y}}_2 \times_{{\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)} {\mathscr{X}}_2$. Therefore, the functor $\Phi$ fits into a distinguished triangle \begin{equation*} \Phi_{p_{{\mathbb{Y}}_2}^*({\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(-1)) \boxtimes p_{{\mathscr{X}}_2}^*({\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(1))} \to \Phi_{j_*{\mathscr{O}}_{{{\mathbb{Y}}_2} \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2)}} \to \Phi. \end{equation*} It follows from~\eqref{diagram:yy-cx3} that \begin{equation*} j^*(p_{{\mathbb{Y}}_2}^*({\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(-1)) \boxtimes p_{{\mathscr{X}}_2}^*({\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(1))) \cong {\mathscr{O}}_{{{\mathbb{Y}}_2} \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2)}, \end{equation*} hence by~\cite{anno2012adjunction} the above triangle of functors is induced by (a rotation of the twist of) the triangle associated with the standard exact sequence \begin{equation*} 0 \to {\mathscr{I}}_{{{\mathbb{Y}}_2} \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2), {{\mathbb{Y}}_2} \times_{{\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)} {{\mathscr{X}}_2}} \to {\mathscr{O}}_{{{\mathbb{Y}}_2} \times_{{\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)} {{\mathscr{X}}_2}} \to j_*{\mathscr{O}}_{{{\mathbb{Y}}_2} \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2)} \to 0. \end{equation*} It finally proves, that up to an irrelevant shift, the functor $\Phi$ is indeed a Fourier--Mukai functor with the kernel \begin{equation} {\mathbb{E}}_2 := {\mathscr{I}}_{{{\mathbb{Y}}_2} \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2), {{\mathbb{Y}}_2} \times_{{\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)} {{\mathscr{X}}_2}} \otimes (p_{{\mathbb{Y}}_2}^*({\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(-1)) \boxtimes p_{{\mathscr{X}}_2}^*({\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(1))) \in {\mathbf{D}}({{\mathbb{Y}}_2} \times_{{\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)} {\mathscr{X}}_2), \end{equation} and thus completes the proof of the theorem.

Universal hyperplane section and linear HPD decomposition
nodes.statement: Let ${{\mathscr{X}}_2} \subset {{\mathbb{X}}_2} \times {\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)$ be the universal hyperplane section of ${{\mathbb{X}}_2}$. By~\cite[Theorem~8.2]{kuznetsov2007hpd}, there is a semiorthogonal decomposition \begin{equation} {\mathbf{D}}({{\mathscr{X}}_2}) = \langle i_*\phi^*({\mathbf{D}}({{\mathbb{Y}}_2})), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(1,1), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(2,2) \rangle, \end{equation} where the morphisms $i$ and $\phi$ are defined by the Cartesian diagram \begin{equation} \vcenter{\xymatrix{ {{\mathbb{Y}}_2} \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2) \ar[r]^-i \ar[d]_\phi & {{\mathscr{X}}_2} \ar[d]^{p_{{\mathscr{X}}_2}} \\ {{\mathbb{Y}}_2} \ar[r]^-{p_{{\mathbb{Y}}_2}} & {\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee) \ar[r]^-{p_2} & {\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee) }} \end{equation} and the map $p_{{\mathbb{Y}}_2}$ is induced by the embedding ${\mathscr{W}}_2^\perp \hookrightarrow {\mathbb{W}}^\vee \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}$.

nodes.name: Rewrite using collection on P(W_1)
nodes.statement: We modify~\eqref{eq:dbxx3-1} by a sequence of mutations to change it to the form we need. First, using the standard exceptional collection ${\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}(W_1)) = \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(-1), {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}, {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(1) \rangle$, decomposition \eqref{eq:dbxx3-1} can be rewritten as \begin{multline*} {\mathbf{D}}({{\mathscr{X}}_2}) = \langle i_*\phi^*({\mathbf{D}}({{\mathbb{Y}}_2})), \\ {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(0,1), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(1,1), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(2,1), \\ {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(1,2), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(2,2), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(3,2) \rangle. \end{multline*}

nodes.name: Mutate last component
nodes.statement: Mutating the last component to the far left and taking into account that $\omega_{{\mathscr{X}}_2} \cong {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(-2,-2)$ up to a line bundle pulled back from ${\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)$, we obtain a semiorthogonal decomposition \begin{multline*} {\mathbf{D}}({{\mathscr{X}}_2}) = \langle {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(1,0), i_*\phi^*({\mathbf{D}}({{\mathbb{Y}}_2})), \\ {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(0,1), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(1,1), \\ {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(2,1), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(1,2), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(2,2) \rangle. \end{multline*}

nodes.name: Mutate second component
nodes.statement: Next, mutating the second component one step to the left, we get \begin{multline} {\mathbf{D}}({{\mathscr{X}}_2}) = \langle \Phi({\mathbf{D}}({{\mathbb{Y}}_2})), \\ {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(1,0), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(0,1), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(1,1), \\ {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(2,1), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(1,2), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(2,2) \rangle. \end{multline} where $\Phi = {\mathbb{L}}_{{\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(1,0)} \circ i_* \circ \phi^* \colon {\mathbf{D}}({{\mathbb{Y}}_2}) \to {\mathbf{D}}({{\mathscr{X}}_2})$.

nodes.statement: {\mathbf{D}}({{\mathscr{X}}_2}) = \langle \Phi({\mathbf{D}}({{\mathbb{Y}}_2})), \\ {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(1,0), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(0,1), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(1,1), \\ {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(2,1), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(1,2), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(2,2) \rangle.

nodes.name: Remains: Phi is Fourier-Mukai supported on fiber product
nodes.statement: This almost proves the result. The only small thing left is to show that the functor $\Phi$ is a Fourier--Mukai functor whose kernel is supported on the fiber product ${{\mathbb{Y}}_2} \times_{{\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)} {{\mathscr{X}}_2}$.

nodes.name: Kernel of i_* phi^*
nodes.statement: For this we note that by~\eqref{diagram:yy-cx3} the functor $i_* \circ \phi^*$ is a Fourier--Mukai functor with kernel $j_*{\mathscr{O}}_{{{\mathbb{Y}}_2} \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2)}$, where $j \colon {\mathbb{Y}}_2 \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2) \to {\mathbb{Y}}_2 \times_{{\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)} {\mathscr{X}}_2$ is the embedding induced by the commutative square~\eqref{diagram:yy-cx3}.

nodes.name: Kernel of the projection composite
nodes.statement: Moreover, using notation from the diagram~\eqref{diagram:yy-cx3}, the projection functor onto ${\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_2}(1,0)$ is given by \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{F}} \mapsto p_{{\mathscr{X}}_2}^*(p_2^*p_{2*}(p_{{\mathscr{X}}_2*}{\mathscr{F}} \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(-1)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(1)), \end{equation*} and its composition with $i_* \circ \phi^*$ is given by \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{F}} \mapsto p_{{\mathscr{X}}_2}^*(p_2^*p_{2*}(p_{{\mathbb{Y}}_2*}{\mathscr{F}} \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(-1)) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(1)). \end{equation*} In other words, this composition is a Fourier--Mukai functor with kernel $p_{{\mathbb{Y}}_2}^*({\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(-1)) \boxtimes p_{{\mathscr{X}}_2}^*({\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(1))$ on ${\mathbb{Y}}_2 \times_{{\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)} {\mathscr{X}}_2$.

nodes.name: Distinguished triangle of functors
nodes.statement: Therefore, the functor $\Phi$ fits into a distinguished triangle \begin{equation*} \Phi_{p_{{\mathbb{Y}}_2}^*({\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(-1)) \boxtimes p_{{\mathscr{X}}_2}^*({\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(1))} \to \Phi_{j_*{\mathscr{O}}_{{{\mathbb{Y}}_2} \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2)}} \to \Phi. \end{equation*}

nodes.statement: It follows from~\eqref{diagram:yy-cx3} that \begin{equation*} j^*(p_{{\mathbb{Y}}_2}^*({\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(-1)) \boxtimes p_{{\mathscr{X}}_2}^*({\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(1))) \cong {\mathscr{O}}_{{{\mathbb{Y}}_2} \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2)}, \end{equation*} hence by~\cite{anno2012adjunction} the above triangle of functors is induced by (a rotation of the twist of) the triangle associated with the standard exact sequence \begin{equation*} 0 \to {\mathscr{I}}_{{{\mathbb{Y}}_2} \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2), {{\mathbb{Y}}_2} \times_{{\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)} {{\mathscr{X}}_2}} \to {\mathscr{O}}_{{{\mathbb{Y}}_2} \times_{{\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)} {{\mathscr{X}}_2}} \to j_*{\mathscr{O}}_{{{\mathbb{Y}}_2} \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2)} \to 0. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Kernel E_2
nodes.statement: It finally proves, that up to an irrelevant shift, the functor $\Phi$ is indeed a Fourier--Mukai functor with the kernel \begin{equation} {\mathbb{E}}_2 := {\mathscr{I}}_{{{\mathbb{Y}}_2} \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2), {{\mathbb{Y}}_2} \times_{{\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)} {{\mathscr{X}}_2}} \otimes (p_{{\mathbb{Y}}_2}^*({\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(-1)) \boxtimes p_{{\mathscr{X}}_2}^*({\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(1))) \in {\mathbf{D}}({{\mathbb{Y}}_2} \times_{{\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)} {\mathscr{X}}_2), \end{equation} and thus completes the proof of the theorem.

nodes.statement: We could, of course, exchange the role of $W_1$ and $W_2$ in the construction. Then we would get a slightly different homological projectively dual variety as the result, that is \begin{equation*} {\mathbb{Y}}_2' = {\mathbb{P}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_2)}(W_1^\vee \otimes \Omega_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_2)}(1)). \end{equation*} Note that the natural maps ${\mathbb{Y}}_2 \to {\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)$ and ${\mathbb{Y}}_2' \to {\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee)$ are birational onto the same discriminant cubic hypersurface ${\mathscr{D}}_{W_1,W_2} \subset {\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{W}}^\vee) = {\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)$ and provide two small resolutions of singularities of~${\mathscr{D}}_{W_1,W_2}$, related to each other by a flop, identifying their derived categories. So, the homological projectively dual of ${\mathbb{X}}_2$ as a category is unambiguously defined, but has two different geometric models~${\mathbb{Y}}_2$ and~${\mathbb{Y}}_2'$, breaking down its inner symmetry.

nodes.statement: Note that $\mathrm{Fl}(W)$ is a smooth hyperplane section of ${\mathbb{P}}(W) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W^\vee)$ corresponding to the natural bilinear pairing $b_0$ between $W$ and~$W^\vee$.

nodes.name: Flag variety Fl(W) as hyperplane section; pairing b_0

nodes.statement: Since~$b_0$ is nondegenerate, it does not lie in the image ${\mathscr{D}}_{W,W^\vee}$ of ${\mathbb{Y}}_2$ in ${\mathbb{P}}(W \otimes W^\vee)$, hence by homological projective duality \cite[Theorem~6.3]{kuznetsov2007hpd} we obtain a semiorthogonal decomposition \begin{equation*} {\mathbf{D}}(\mathrm{Fl}(W)) = \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathrm{Fl}(W)}(0,-1), {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathrm{Fl}(W)}(-1,0), {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathrm{Fl}(W)}, {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathrm{Fl}(W)}(1,0), {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathrm{Fl}(W)}(0,1), {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathrm{Fl}(W)}(1,1) \rangle. \end{equation*} Clearly, this is a Lefschetz collection with respect to ${\mathscr{O}}_{\mathrm{Fl}(W)}(1,1)$ with two blocks equal to \begin{equation} {\mathcal{A}}_{\mathrm{Fl}(W)}^{\rm{sym}} = \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathrm{Fl}(W)}(0,-1), {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathrm{Fl}(W)}(-1,0), {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathrm{Fl}(W)} \rangle. \end{equation}

nodes.statement: Denote by $V_1$, $V_2$, and $V_3$ three two-dimensional vector spaces, consider the product \begin{equation*} {{\mathbb{X}}_3} := {\mathbb{P}}(V_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_2) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_3), \end{equation*} its Segre embedding ${\mathbb{X}}_3 \hookrightarrow {\mathbb{P}}(V_1 \otimes V_2 \otimes V_3) =: {\mathbb{P}}({\mathbb{V}})$, and the standard exceptional collection on ${{\mathbb{X}}_3}$: \begin{equation*} {\mathbf{D}}({{\mathbb{X}}_3}) = \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_3}, {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_3}(1,0,0), {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_3}(0,1,0), {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_3}(1,1,0), {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_3}(0,0,1), {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_3}(1,0,1), {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_3}(0,1,1), {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_3}(1,1,1) \rangle. \end{equation*}
nodes.name: X_3 = (P^1)^3 and its standard collection

nodes.statement: We modify this collection slightly to turn it into a symmetric rectangular Lefschetz decomposition with respect to the line bundle ${\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_3}(1,1,1)$. For this we mutate ${\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_3}(1,1,0)$, ${\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_3}(1,0,1)$ and ${\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_3}(0,1,1)$ to the far right. An easy computation shows that what we get is an exceptional collection \begin{equation*} {\mathbf{D}}({{\mathbb{X}}_3}) = \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_3}, {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_3}(1,0,0), {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_3}(0,1,0), {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_3}(0,0,1), {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_3}(1,1,1), {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_3}(2,1,1), {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_3}(1,2,1), {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_3}(1,1,2) \rangle. \end{equation*} Clearly, this is a rectangular Lefschetz collection with respect to ${\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_3}(1,1,1)$ with two blocks equal to \begin{equation} {\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_3}^{\rm{sym}} = \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_3}, {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_3}(1,0,0), {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_3}(0,1,0), {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_3}(0,0,1) \rangle. \end{equation} It is symmetric with respect to the action of the group ${\mathfrak{S}}_3$ by permutations of factors.
nodes.name: Symmetric rectangular Lefschetz decomposition of (P^1)^3
nodes.statement_short: Mutating O(1,1,0), O(1,0,1), O(0,1,1) to the right gives a rectangular Lefschetz collection with two blocks <O, O(1,0,0), O(0,1,0), O(0,0,1)>.
conclusions: It is symmetric with respect to the action of the group ${\mathfrak{S}}_3$ by permutations of factors

nodes.statement: {\mathcal{A}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_3}^{\rm{sym}} = \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_3}, {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_3}(1,0,0), {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_3}(0,1,0), {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{X}}_3}(0,0,1) \rangle.

nodes.statement: Again, the scheme ${\mathbb{X}}_3$ can be represented as a projectivization of a vector bundle \begin{equation*} {{\mathbb{X}}_3} \cong {\mathbb{P}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_2)}({\mathscr{V}}_3), \qquad {\mathscr{V}}_3 := V_3\otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_2)}(-1,-1) \subset {\mathbb{V}} \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_2)}. \end{equation*} Consequently, by~\cite[Corollary~8.3]{kuznetsov2007hpd} the homological projectively dual of ${{\mathbb{X}}_3}$ with respect to the Lefschetz decomposition with the first block ${\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}(V_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_2))$ is \begin{equation} {{\mathbb{Y}}_3} := {\mathbb{P}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_2)}({\mathscr{V}}_3^\perp), \end{equation} where ${\mathscr{V}}_3^\perp := \mathrm{Ker}({\mathbb{V}}^\vee \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_2)} \to {\mathscr{V}}_3^\vee) \cong V_3^\vee \otimes \Omega_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1 \otimes V_2)}(1) \vert_{{\mathbb{P}}(V_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_2)}$ is a rank 6 vector bundle on~${\mathbb{P}}(V_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(V_2)$.
